# Mechanistic Studies and Identification of Catalyst Deactivation Pathways for Pyridine(diimine) Iron Catalyzed C(sp2)–H Borylation

**Authors:** Tianyi Zhang; Tyler P. Pabst; Jordan M. Hoyt; Matthew V. Pecoraro; Paul J. Chirik

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States

## Abstract

The synthesis and application of aryl-substituted pyridine(diimine) iron complexes (RPDI)FeCH3 to the catalytic borylation of heteroarenes under thermal conditions is described. Improvements in catalyst design and performance were guided by precatalyst activation studies, where investigations into stoichiometric reactivities of iron borohydride (4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe(H2BPin) and iron furyl (4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe(2-methylfuryl) complexes revealed facile C(sp2)–H activation and a slower and potentially turnover-limiting C(sp2)–B formation step. Formation of the flyover dimer, [(4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe]2 was identified as a catalyst deactivation pathway and formally iron(0) complexes were found to be inactive for borylation. The pyridine(diimine) iron borohydride, flyover dimer and furyl complexes were characterized by X-ray diffraction and their electronic structures determined by a combination of NMR, EPR, and Mössbauer spectroscopies corroborated by DFT calculations. The role of the redox-active pyridine(diimine) ligand in catalytic C–H borylation was also investigated.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

The functionalization of C–H bonds is a step-economical strategy that has been a longstanding challenge in synthetic chemistry.1 Among the various methods, C–H borylation is particularly desirable as the resultant boronic esters are synthetic lynchpins for a host of C–C and C–X bond forming reactions.2 Specifically, iridium-catalyzed C–H borylation, independently developed by Hartwig and Smith,3,4 is one of the most widely applied C–H functionalization methods owing to high activity, predictable sterically driven site selectivity, and functional group compatibility.5 The accepted pathway for iridium-catalyzed C(sp2)–H borylation with bipyridine-type ligands involves an Ir(III)–Ir(V) redox cycle with turnover-limiting C(sp2)–H oxidative addition from an iridium(III) tris(boryl) resting state (Figure 1a).3b,6

Interest has intensified for the discovery and adoption of catalysts with more earth-abundant metals for C–H functionalization.7,8 The relatively high density of states and access to open shell intermediates with first row transition metals offer the opportunity for distinct reactivity but also poses challenges for developing the fundamental organometallic chemistry to promote the desired transformations.9 In addition to examples of cobalt-catalyzed C(sp2)–H borylation reported by Driess, Smith and others,10 our group has developed a family of pincer-supported cobalt complexes for the borylation of arenes and heteroarenes (Figure 1b).11 In the cases examined, the experimental and computational data support a Co(I)–Co(III) redox couple where C(sp2)–H oxidative addition occurs from a cobalt(I)-boryl intermediate. The relative rate of the C(sp2)–H activation step compared to others in the cycle is catalyst and substrate dependent. With pincers with phosphine donors, electron-poor substrates such as fluoroarenes undergo fast and reversible C(sp2)–H oxidative addition while for more electron-rich examples such as 2,6-lutidine, C(sp2)–H oxidative addition is turnover limiting.10,12 In addition, the nickel-catalyzed C(sp2)–H borylation of (hetero)arenes has also been studied by several groups,13 with nickel nanoparticles proposed as the active catalyst in some cases.

Concerns over the toxicity of cobalt and nickel and the sourcing of the former inspire the development of catalysts based on iron.7d,14,15 Despite an initial report by Hartwig and coworkers on stoichiometric, photochemical borylation of C(sp2)–H bonds promoted by CpFe(CO)2–BCat in 1995 (Figure 1c),16 iron-catalyzed C–H borylation remains in the early stages of development with limited mechanistic understanding.17 Under photochemical conditions, Mankad and coworkers reported the heterobimetallic (Cp)(CO)2Fe–Cu-(NHC) catalyst, where catalyst deactivation by Fp2 dimer (Fp = (Cp)(CO)2Fe) formation is circumvented by Fe–Cu bond formation upon H2 elimination.18 Using monometallic bis-(phosphine) iron(II) dimethyl precatalysts, Darcel and coworkers reported arene C(sp2)–H borylation with a proposed mechanism featuring Fe(0)–Fe(II) redox cycling, while Thomas and coworkers demonstrated the viability of in situ catalyst generation from the corresponding bis(phosphine) iron(II) chloride.17

For thermal iron-catalyzed C–H borylation (Figure 1c), Okhi, Tatsumi, and coworkers demonstrated facile C(sp2)–H activation and C–B bond formation mediated by Cp(NHC)Fe alkyl/aryl complexes and identified iron borohydride formation as a catalyst deactivation pathway.17,20 Kamitani and coworkers proposed redox-neutral C–H activation by a putative iron bisalkoxide complex supported by PNN ligands.17 In addition to an off-cycle dimeric iron hydride complex, Nishibayashi and coworkers identified a catalytically active square planar (PNP)FeII–X (X = H, BPin, furyl) complexes (PNP = bisphosphinopyrrolide) capable of C(sp2)–H activation and C–B bond formation at 100 °C.17c,21

To date, iron-catalyzed C–H borylation has been dominated by complexes supported by strong-field ligands such as cyclopentadienyls, phosphines and/or N-heterocyclic carbenes. Alternatives with weaker field, potentially redox-active chelates remain underexplored (Figure 2a). This latter class of iron compounds is attractive given the synthetic and electronic modularity of pyridine(diimine) (PDI) iron complexes,22 the precedent for engaging in bond activation chemistry involving metal–ligand cooperativity,19,23 and distinct redox flexibility.24 In addition, while the mechanism of iridium- and cobalt-catalyzed C(sp2)–H borylation has been well-studied,6,11 there is limited understanding of how iron catalysts operate. Open questions include the nature and oxidation state of the iron intermediate responsible for C–H activation, the role of redox cycling during catalytic turnover and the origin of catalyst deactivation. Gaining insights into these fundamental processes is essential for increasing both the activity and synthetic utility of iron catalysts for C–H borylation.

Here we describe the synthesis and evaluation of pyridine-(diimine) iron alkyl complexes for the catalytic C(sp2)–H borylation of heteroarenes (Figure 2b). Catalyst deactivation pathways were identified that enabled improvements in catalyst performance. Catalytically active iron intermediates including borohydride (4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe(H2BPin) and furyl (4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe(2-methylfuryl) complexes were identified as well as the off-cycle, flyover dimer, [(4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe]2 by a combination of X-ray diffraction, NMR, EPR, and Mössbauer spectroscopies. Stoichiometric studies were used to establish key elementary organometallic steps as well as the identification of the resting state and the turnover limiting step.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

### Initial Evaluation of the Reactivity of (PDI)FeCH3 Precatalysts in Catalytic C(sp2)–H Borylation.

The pyridine(diimine) iron methyl complex, 1–CH3 was evaluated for the catalytic borylation of 2-methylfuran (6). Standard conditions employed 10 equiv of 6, 1 equiv of HBPin, 5 mol % of the iron methyl complex at 50 °C for 16 h. This procedure generated the 5-borylated furan product (7) in 47% yield as quantified by 1H NMR spectroscopy versus an internal standard (Scheme 1a).

The observation of borylation activity motivated additional investigations into the potential intermediacy of an iron boryl complex and determination of its electronic structure, specifically if there is any involvement of the redox activity of the pyridine(diimine) chelate. Addition of one equivalent of HBPin to a benzene-d6 solution of 1–CH3 resulted in immediate consumption of the organometallic iron complex with concomitant formation of methane as determined by 1H NMR spectroscopy (Scheme 1b). Monitoring the reaction over time produced new resonances signaling gradual formation of a pyridine(diimine) iron dinitrogen complex, assigned as 5–(N2)2 where the 4-position of the pyridine ring has undergone C–H borylation. Resubjecting 5–(N2)2 to analogous reaction conditions with 2-methylfuran did not produce any observable borylation.

Based on these observations and the lack of evidence for benzene-d6 borylation by NMR spectroscopy or gas chromatography, a pathway whereby the transfer of the boryl to the pyridine(diimine) ligand was considered. Similar borylation reactivity and deactivation was observed with [(iPrPNP)Co] catalysts (PNP = bisphosphinopyridine).11b A plausible pathway involves reaction of 1–CH3 with HBPin to generate methane along with a transient iron-boryl complex that in turn undergoes intermolecular C(sp2)–H activation at 4-position of the PDI pyridine ring to afford the corresponding iron hydride (5–H). Such reactivity was observed with cobalt pincer borylation catalysts.11b Rapid bimolecular reductive elimination of H2 in the presence of N2 forms the dinitrogen complex 5–(N2)2 (Scheme 1b), analogous to the reactivity of the corresponding pyridine(diimine) iron methyl complexes.24

### Catalytic Performance of 4-Substituted (PDI)Fe Complexes for C(sp2)–H Borylation.

The competing borylation of the 4-position of the pyridine(diimine) ligand prompted the exploration of iron methyl compounds with substituents designed to block ligand modification (Scheme 1c). The catalytic C(sp2)–H borylation with each of the pyridine(diimine)iron methyl complexes was evaluated with 6 as a representative substrate (Table 1). Using bis(pinacolato)-diboron (B2Pin2) as the boron reagent,25 heating 5 mol % of 1–CH3 in neat 6 at 50 °C furnished the 5-borylated product (7) in 47% yield (entry 1). A significant increase in yield to 170% (out of a theoretical maximum of 200%) was observed with 2–CH3 as the precatalyst (entry 2), establishing the impact of the 4-substituent. An 80% yield of 7 was obtained with 2–CH3 and one equivalent of HBPin (entry 5), demonstrating that the HBPin byproduct formed from C(sp2)–H borylation with B2Pin2 is also an effective borylating reagent. This accounts for the theoretical maximum yield of 200% (relative to B2Pin2 equivalence) for borylation with B2Pin2.

Replacing the 4-tert-butyl group on the pyridine of the chelate with a more electron-donating pyrrolidinyl substituent did not lead to significant changes in catalytic performance, as similar yields were observed with 2–CH3 and 3–CH3 using either B2Pin2 (entries 2 and 3) or HBPin (entries 5 and 6) as the boron reagent. This suggests limited opportunities for modifying the electron-donating ability of the pyridine-(diimine) ligand for additional catalyst improvement. Reducing the size of the 2,6-aryl substituents from 2,6-diisopropyl (2–CH3) to 2,6-dimethyl (4–CH3) on the N-imine resulted in a loss of catalytic activity (entries 4 and 7), suggesting that the more sterically accessible iron center results in more rapid deactivation rather than improved performance. These results are consistent with recent findings that larger aryl imine substituents impart greater kinetic stability to (PDI)FeCH3 complexes.24

Pyridine(diimine) iron complexes in the formal iron(0) oxidation state were also investigated as precatalysts for the C(sp2)–H borylation of 6 given their well-precedented catalytic activity.26 The iron bis(dinitrogen) complex, 2–(N2)2 as well as the iron methyl ate complex, [2–CH3]– were evaluated (entries 8 and 9) and no appreciable activity was observed in either case. The results suggest that oxidative addition to formally iron(0) compounds is not operative and also provides insight into the inactivity of the more open iron methyl complexes as these are known to undergo rapid bimolecular elimination of ethane to form formally iron(0) compounds. Attempts to borylate thiophenes, pyrroles, oxazoles and pyridines were unsuccessful, producing only trace quantities of the organoboronate ester.27

### Stoichiometric Reactivity of (4-tBu-iPrPDI)FeCH3 Complexes with Boron Reagents.

The observation of catalytic borylation activity with pyridine(diimine) iron methyl complexes prompted more detailed studies into the mechanism of the reaction. To study activation of the iron precatalyst, a benzene-d6 solution of 2–CH3 was treated with one equivalent of HBPin (Scheme 2). Complete consumption of the iron methyl complex was observed within 5 min and the formation of CH3BPin was confirmed by 1H and 11B NMR spectroscopies. Addition of excess HBPin formed a red-brown solution with paramagnetically broadened and shifted 1H NMR resonances. The iron product was identified as the pyridine(diimine) iron borohydride complex, 2–(H2BPin) based on single-crystal X-ray diffraction (vide infra). 2–(H2BPin) is likely formed by capture of the iron hydride intermediate 2–H by HBPin.

In the absence of excess HBPin, 2–(H2BPin) was consumed with concomitant formation of HBPin, H2 and the reported iron dinitrogen complex 2–(N2)2.28 A separate recrystallization following the treatment of 2–CH3 with one equivalent of HBPin in pentane at −35 °C produced dark green crystals that were identified as the iron flyover dimer, 2–Dimer as determined by X-ray diffraction. Dissolution of 2–Dimer in benzene-d6 under N2 atmosphere led to the formation of 2–(N2)2 as determined by 1H NMR spectroscopy, while subjecting 2–(N2)2 to analogous recrystallization conditions did not furnish 2–Dimer, demonstrating irreversible conversion to the iron dinitrogen complex 2–(N2)2. In a control experiment, a benzene-d6 solution of 2–(N2)2 was treated with 2 equiv of HBPin at ambient or elevated temperatures and neither the consumption of 2–(N2)2 nor the formation of 2–(H2BPin) was observed by 1H NMR spectroscopy. Similarly, addition of excess HBPin to 2-Dimer at room or elevated temperature did not yield observable quantities of 2-(H2BPin). Notably, activation of C(sp2)–H, B–H, and B–B bonds was sluggish with either 2–Dimer or 2–(N2)2 at both room and elevated temperatures.

Treatment of a benzene-d6 solution of 2–CH3 with 1 equiv of B2Pin2 at ambient temperature resulted in complete consumption of the iron methyl complex within 5 min along with formation of 2–(N2)2, CH3BPin and HBPin. No evidence was obtained for borylation of the solvent. Recrystallization from pentane at −35 °C resulted in isolation of 2–Dimer. It is posited that an iron-boryl complex, 2–BPin is initially formed from the reaction between 2–CH3 and B2Pin2 and in the absence of a suitably activated C(sp2)–H bond, 2–BPin undergoes the loss of boryl as B2Pin2 to form 2–Dimer. One possibility is the ejection of boryl radical though this is unlikely given the relatively strong DFT-computed Fe–B bond of 49.1 kcal/mol (see Scheme S2). In comparison to the isolable, 4-coordinate and idealized planar (PNP)Fe(II) boryl complex (PNP = bisphosphinopyrrolide) reported by Nishibayashi and coworkers,17c the transient nature of the (PDI)Fe–boryl complex supports the role of the strong-field pincer in stabilizing the iron boryl intermediate through stronger Fe to B π-backbonding. Moreover, this is consistent with DFT calculations (Scheme S2) which suggest a substantially weaker Fe–B bond in the 2–BPin intermediate (BDFE = 49.1 kcal/mol) than in Nishibayashi’s (PNP)FeBPin (BDFE = 68.3 kcal/mol). Taken together, the stoichiometric experiments demonstrate that the coordination of HBPin to 2–H is reversible and that the formation of the 2–Dimer is a catalyst deactivation pathway for [(PDI)Fe] class of borylation catalysts.

### Characterization of Pyridine(diimine) Iron Complexes Relevant to Catalytic C(sp2)–H Borylation.

The solid-state structure of (4-tBu-iPrPDI)Fe(κ2–H2BPin) was determined by single crystal X-ray diffraction (Figure 3a) and confirmed the identity of the compound. Two bridging hydrogen atoms were located in the difference map and established the presence of an LX-type borohydride ligand rather than an X-type boryl. The Fe–B bond distance of 2.158(3) Å is significantly longer than the sum of the van der Waals radii of iron and boron (2.05 Å) and those of known iron boryl complexes,17,29 but falls within the range of those in known FeII–H–B complexes (1.855(2) to 2.319(3) Å),30 further supporting the assignment as the iron borohydride.

Notably, the iron borohydride 2–(H2BPin) is related to the cobalt(III) dihydridoboryl complexes, L3Co(H)2(BPin) reported by our laboratory that are precatalysts for C(sp2)–H borylation.31 With iron, the less electron donating and redox-active pyridine(diimine) favors reductive coupling and hence the five-coordinate iron borohydride 2–(H2BPin) and raises the question about the role of redox cycling in catalytic borylation.

To investigate the electronic structure of 2–(H2BPin), the solid-state, zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectrum was collected and exhibits a single quadrupole doublet with an isomer shift (δ) of 0.29 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting (|ΔEQ|) of 1.54 mm/s (Figure 3b). The DFT computed isomer shift of 0.37 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting of 1.82 mm/s are in agreement with the experimental data and support a BS(2,1) electronic structure description for 2–(H2BPin), featuring an intermediate-spin Fe center (SFe = 1) with a monoreduced PDI ligand.32 The X-band EPR spectrum was recorded at 10 K and features a rhombic signal with g-values of 2.73, 2.07, 2.02 (Figure 3c), consistent with a metal centered radical in an overall S = 1/2 complex. The spin density plot for the BS(2,1) electronic structure description of 2–(H2BPin) (Figure 3d) revealed spin delocalization on the imine and pyridine portion of the PDI ligand. Thus, the overall S = 1/2 ground state is best described as an intermediate spin iron(II) complex (SFe = 1) engaged in antiferromagnetic coupling with a pyridine-(diimine)-centered radical. While known iron borohydrides are diamagnetic,17,33 2–(H2BPin) represents a rare example of a paramagnetic iron borohydride derivative.

The flyover dimer, 2–Dimer was also characterized by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. In the solid state, overall idealized C2 symmetry was observed between the two iron centers and the supporting pyridine (diimine) ligands (Figure 4a). Each iron center (e.g., Fe1) has one imine N atom (e.g., N4) and one pyridine N atom (N5) coordinated from one PDI ligand, while the imine C=N double bond on the second PDI ligand (e.g., N1 and C13) is η2 coordinated to the same iron center, likely to maximize π-backbonding. Accordingly, the N(1)–C(13) bond is elongated to 1.389(4) Å as compared to the N(4)–C(61) bond length of 1.335(4) Å (Figure 4b). A significant distortion from planarity is also observed around each iron center (τ4′ = 0.462) as each iron atom is raised out of the pincer plane, as evidenced by the bond angles around the iron center. The two iron centers are separated by 4.255 Å, rendering metal–metal bonding unlikely. In benzene-d6, 2–Dimer was NMR silent as no resonances were observed that could be assigned to the compound. This behavior likely arises from magnetic coupling between the two iron centers through the pyridine(diimine) ligands or due to dynamic behavior of the dimer in solution.

Iron hydrides were considered as possibilities for the structure of 2–Dimer. While the paramagnetism of the sample precludes reliable, direct observation by NMR spectroscopy, the lack of reactivity with HBPin, B2Pin2 or 2-methylfuran supports their absence.34 Likewise, no bands diagnostic of Fe–H stretches35 were observed in the infrared spectrum. While circumstantial and principally negative evidence, the combined data supports the formulation as the dimer of [(PDI)Fe].

The zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectrum of 2–Dimer was recorded in the solid state at 80 K and exhibits an isomer shift of 0.63 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting of 1.14 mm/s (Figure 4c). The observed isomer shift is consistent with reported values (0.49–0.57 mm/s) for high-spin (S = 2) iron(II) complexes with pyridine(diimine) ligands.24 The observed quadrupole splitting is consistent with the reported value (1.17 mm/s) for a related CS-symmetric dinuclear (PDI)Fe(II) complex formed from the corresponding PDI iron methyl complex by bimolecular reductive elimination of ethane.36 No signal was observed when collecting the X-band EPR spectrum of 2–Dimer in toluene glass at 10 K. Furthermore, the DFT-calculated relative energies, Mössbauer parameters (δ = 0.56 mm/s, |ΔEQ|=0.84 mm/s, Table S1) and metrical parameters suggest that the electronic structure of 2-Dimer is best described as two high-spin (S = 2) Fe(II) centers engaged in antiferromagnetically coupling, corroborating the C2-symmetry observed in the solid-state structure.

### Isolation of Catalytically Relevant Iron Complexes: Identification of Facile C(sp2)–H Activation and Slow C(sp2)–B Bond Formation.

With the identification of the precatalyst activation and catalyst deactivation pathway, the stoichiometric reactivity of pyridine(diimine) iron complexes in C(sp2)–H activation was investigated using 6 as a representative substrate. Addition of one equivalent of B2Pin2 to a benzene-d6 solution of 2–CH3 in the presence of 2 equiv of 2-methylfuran at room temperature resulted in the formation of a new paramagnetic product identified as the iron furyl complex, 2–(2-Me)Furyl. The expected organic byproduct, CH3BPin was also observed by NMR spectroscopy (Scheme 3a). Performing a related experiment with one equivalent of HBPin also resulted in clean conversion to 2–(2-Me)Furyl, which was then isolated as dark brown crystals in 91% yield, following recrystallization in a pentane/toluene solution at −35 °C. In contrast, 2–CH3 did not react with 2-methylfuran in the absence of boron reagents at room temperature. Heating a benzene-d6 solution of 2–CH3 to 65 °C for 24 h in the presence of 10 equiv of 2-methylfuran furnished 2–(2-Me)Furyl, demonstrating a lower barrier for C(sp2)–H activation by iron boryls over iron alkyls.

Addition of one equivalent of 2-methylfuran to a benzene-d6 solution of 2–(H2BPin) at ambient temperature resulted in clean and quantitative formation of 2–(2-Me)Furyl, consistent with reversible HBPin dissociation from 2–(H2BPin) to generate an intermediate iron hydride 2–H responsible for C(sp2)–H activation (Scheme 3b). In contrast, the iron borohydride, (η5-C5Me5)(NHC)Fe(H2BPin), isolated by Okhi and Tatsumi, contains a substantially shorter Fe–B distance of 2.002(3) Å than the value of 2.158(3) Å in 2–(H2BPin) and is inactive for catalytic borylation (Figure 3a).17a This reactivity difference is likely a result of a higher barrier for HBPin dissociation to generate the active iron hydride, a consequence of stronger π-backbonding from a more electron-rich iron(II) center arising from more electron-donating ligands.

Taken together, the stoichiometric studies demonstrate that C(sp2)–H activation by the pyridine(diimine) iron hydride (2–H) or boryl (2-BPin) has a lower activation barrier than that by the corresponding iron methyl (2–CH3) complex and is more likely to be the dominant pathway under catalytic conditions. Similar trends in relative rates of C(sp2)–H activation have been observed in reported (PNP)Co–X (X = H, alkyl, and BPin) complexes (PNP = bisphosphinopyridine).11

Single-turnover experiments were carried out to determine the catalytic competency of 2–(2-Me)Furyl (Scheme 3c). Addition of one equivalent of B2Pin2 to a benzene-d6 solution of 2–(2-Me)Furyl and heating to 50 °C generated the borylated product, 7 in 78% yield. No reaction was observed when the procedure was conducted at ambient temperature. Using HBPin in place of B2Pin2 under analogous conditions produced a similar yield of 71% of 7. Related stoichiometric reactivity was observed for the (PNP)Fe(furyl) complex (PNP = bisphosphinopyrrolide) reported by Nishibayashi and coworkers.17c These results suggest that 2–(2-Me)Furyl is likely on-cycle and catalytically competent. In both cases (B2Pin2 and HBPin), conversion to the iron dinitrogen complex 2–(N2)2 was the only observed iron-containing product by 1H NMR spectroscopy, presumably formed from the transiently generated iron boryl (2–BPin) or hydride (2–H) complexes in the absence of excess furan (Scheme 2). Analysis of the results of the stoichiometric studies suggests that with pyridine(diimine) iron complexes, C(sp2)–B formation incurs a higher activation barrier than C(sp2)–H activation and may be the turnover-limiting step (Scheme 3a,b).

The solid-state structure of 2–(2-Me)Furyl was determined by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and confirms the identity of the molecule as an idealized planar iron complex. An Npyridine–Fe–C angle of 174.44 (14)° is observed and the furanyl ring is rotated by 43° relative to the idealized iron-chelate plane (Figure 5a). The Nimine–Cimine bond distances of 1.326(4) Å and 1.339(4) Å and Cimine–Cipso values of 1.442(4) Å and 1.431(4) Å are consistent with reported values for (PDI)FeX (X = halides, alkyl) and are diagnostic of a monoreduced [(4-tBu-iPrPDI)]1– ligand coordinated to a ferrous center.37

The zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectrum of 2–(2-Me)Furyl was recorded in the solid state at 80 K and exhibits quadrupole doublets with an isomer shift (δ) of 0.30 mm/s and a quadrupole splitting (|ΔEQ|) of 3.68 mm/s (Figure 5b), consistent with the reported values for analogous idealized planar pyridine(diimine) iron alkyl/aryl complexes including: 2–CH3 (δ = 0.31 mm/s, |ΔEQ| = 3.73 mm/s) and (iPrPDI)Fe(2-benzofuryl) (δ = 0.33 mm/s, |ΔEQ| = 3.55 mm/s).24,38 2–(N2) and 2–(N2)2 side products formed during synthesis cocrystallized with 2–(2-Me)Furyl and were also identified in the Mössbauer spectrum.28 The band asymmetry observed for 2–(N2)2 is likely due to sample inhomogeneity or overlapping peaks in the mixture. Spectra of the isolated material do not exhibit this asymmetry.28 The X-band EPR spectrum of 2–(2-Me)Furyl was recorded in toluene glass at 10 K and a rhombic signal was observed and simulated to provide g-values of 3.36, 1.90, and 1.85 (Figure 5c). The simulation is most consistent with an overall S = 1/2 complex with iron-centered radical. A near-idealized planar geometry around the iron center and the Mössbauer and EPR data support an intermediate-spin iron(II) center (SFe = 1) engaged in antiferromagnetically coupling to a monoreduced pyridine(diimine) radical anion (SPDI = 1/2). Thus, the overall C(sp2)–H activation reactions from (PDI)Fe–X (X = H, CH3, BPin) are net redox-neutral as both reactants and products have identical electronic structures.

### Proposed Mechanism for (PDI)Fe-Catalyzed C(sp2)–H Borylation.

With the results of the stoichiometric studies in hand, a mechanism for (PDI)Fe-catalyzed C(sp2)–H borylation was proposed with 6 as a representative substrate and the iron methyl complex 2–CH3 as the precatalyst (Scheme 4). With B2Pin2 as the borylating reagent, activation of 2–CH3 with B2Pin2 forms the putative iron boryl complex 2–BPin. This then undergoes facile C(sp2)–H activation with 2-methylfuran to form the iron furyl complex, 2–(2-Me)Furyl, which is the catalyst resting state. Alternatively, the activation of precatalyst 2–CH3 with HBPin leads to the formation of iron hydride 2–H, which is in equilibrium with the iron borohydride, 2–(H2BPin) in the presence of excess HBPin. Given that HBPin is a byproduct of C(sp2)–H borylation with B2Pin2, both 2–BPin and 2–(H2BPin) are relevant intermediates during catalytic borylation. In the presence of substrate, 2–H also undergoes the C(sp2)–H bond activation with a relatively low barrier to form 2–(2-Me)Furyl. Direct C(sp2)–H activation by 2–CH3 is comparatively sluggish and therefore catalyst initiation is slower than C(sp2)–H bond activation from catalytically active compounds. The isolation of iron(II) borohydride 2–(H2BPin), instead of an iron dihydridoboryl complex analogous to L3CoIII(H)2(BPin),11 suggests that C(sp2)–H activation by (PDI)Fe–X (X = H, CH3, BPin) is less likely to proceed by oxidative addition with Fe(II/III) redox cycling; instead, a redox-neutral mechanism akin to σ-complex-assisted metathesis (σ-CAM) is more plausible.

From the iron furyl complex 2–(2-Me)Furyl, a reaction with B2Pin2 through potentially turnover-limiting C(sp2)–B formation then affords product 7, with the reformation of 2–BPin. Alternatively, 2–(2-Me)Furyl reacts with HBPin to yield product 7 with the regeneration of 2–H (and 2–(H2BPin) when HBPin is in excess). In the absence of excess 6, the competing catalyst deactivation pathway becomes more dominant, where 2–BPin and 2–H undergo the loss of boryl as B2Pin2 and a bimolecular reductive elimination of H2, respectively, to the flyover dimer 2–Dimer and eventually the iron dinitrogen complex 2–(N2)2. Both complexes are catalytically inactive and incapable of reentering the catalytic cycle under standard conditions.

In summary, the evaluation of various pyridine(diimine) iron complexes for the catalytic C(sp2)–H borylation of 2-methylfuran and gaining mechanistic insights through stoichiometric experiments and electronic structure studies have provided a foundation for the development of catalyst design principles (Figure 6). Substitution of the 4-position of the pyridine(diimine) ligand boosts catalytic activity by minimizing competing borylation of this site that in turn leads to catalyst deactivation. The size of the 2,6-aryl substituents is also important for maintaining catalyst performance as larger isopropyl groups stabilize the iron complex from deleterious bimolecular reductive elimination. Notably, formally iron(0) complexes supported by pyridine(diimines) were inactive for borylation, arising from the inability of these compounds to activate HBPin or B2Pin2. Overall, these catalyst design principles would hopefully provide the foundation for the design of next generation iron C–H borylation catalysts.

## CONCLUSIONS

Mechanistic investigations into C(sp2)–H borylation of 2-methylfuran catalyzed by (PDI)FeCH3 precatalysts were conducted. Identification of boryl migration upon activation of (iPrPDI)FeCH3 motivated mechanism-guided catalyst design to circumvent the deactivation pathway by ligand modifications. Following the investigation of the stoichiometric reactivity of [(PDI)Fe] complexes with boron reagents and the C(sp2)–H activation of 2-methylfuran, catalytically active as well as off-cycle [(PDI)Fe] complexes were identified, isolated and their solid-state and electronic structures unambiguously determined by X-ray diffraction, NMR, EPR and Mössbauer spectroscopies as well as computational studies. Based on stoichiometric experiments, the formation of a pyridine(diimine) iron flyover-dimer complex was identified as a catalyst deactivation pathway. C(sp2)–H activation by transient pyridine(diimine) iron hydride and iron boryl complexes was faster than with the corresponding iron methyl, and occurs through a net redox-neutral pathway. Idealized planar, intermediate spin ferrous compounds engaged in antiferromagnetic coupling with a chelate radical anion are persistent throughout. Stoichiometric studies support C–B bond formation as having a higher barrier than C(sp2)–H activation and is therefore the likely turnover-limiting step. These findings provide rare insights into a catalytic borylation process with paramagnetic iron compounds and provide the foundation for next generation catalyst design.

# Redox-Neutral, Iron-Mediated Directed C─H Activation: General Principles and Mechanistic Insights

**Authors:** Tianyi Zhang; William G. Whitehurst; Matthew V. Pecoraro; Junho Kim; Stefan G. Koenig; Paul J. Chirik

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States | Synthetic Molecule Process Chemistry, Genentech Inc, South San Francisco, California 94080, United States

## Abstract

Experimental and computational studies have been conducted and established the general principles for enabling redox-neutral C─H activation by iron(II) complexes. The idealized octahedral iron(II) dimethyl complex, (depe)2Fe(CH3)2 (depe = 1,2-bis(diethylphosphino)ethane) promoted the directed, regioselective ortho C(sp2)─H methylation of pivalophenone. The rate of the iron(II)-mediated C(sp2)─H functionalization depended on the lability of L-type phosphine ligands, the spin state of the iron center, and the size of the X-type ligands (halide, hydrocarbyl) in P4FeIIX2 complexes. The C(sp2)─H alkylation reaction proved general among multiple substrates with directing groups including carbonyl, imines and pyridines. Among these, ketones and aldehydes were identified as optimal and were compatible with various steric environments and presence of acidic α-hydrogens. With stronger nitrogen donors, higher barriers for product-forming reductive elimination were observed. The effect of orbital hybridization on the chemoselectivity of C─H activation through a σ-CAM pathway by dm>0 transition metals was also established by studying the stoichiometric reactivity of the differentially substituted (depe)2Fe(Me)R complexes (R = alkyl, aryl), where the Fe─R bond with greater s-character preferentially promoted selective C─H activation. Deuterium labeling and kinetic studies, coupled with computational analysis, supported a pathway involving phosphine dissociation and rate-determining C─H bond activation, leading to the observed products.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

Methods for selective formation of carbon─carbon bonds directly from C─H bonds are transformative in synthesis and sustainable chemistry as preinstalled functional groups are obviated.1,2 Historically this reactivity has been dominated by precious metal compounds as the strong ligand fields enable the requisite two-electron redox-cycling through oxidative addition and reductive elimination.3 Earth-abundant first-row transition metals are attracting increased attention due to their potential cost and environmental benefits,4 and also offer the opportunity for new and mechanistically distinct reactivity and site selectivity.5 Among these, iron is one of the most attractive for sustainable C─H functionalization due to its low cost,6 high natural abundance,7 and negligible toxicity.8

In addition to enzymatic reactions,9 C─H activation by molecular iron complexes dates to the pioneering work of Miyake and co-workers who demonstrated the intramolecular oxidative addition of aryl C─H bonds of the phosphine ligand in the putative [(dppe)2Fe(0)] complex (dppe = 1,2-bis(diphenylphosphino)ethane) to form the corresponding cyclometalated iron(II) hydride.10 Ittel, Tolman and co-workers extended this reactivity to the intermolecular oxidative addition of activated sp3, aryl and alkynyl C─H bonds to in situ generated [(dmpe)2Fe(0)] (Scheme 1a; dmpe = 1,2-bis(dimethylphosphino)ethane).11 These observations were corroborated by transient and matrix photochemical studies by Perutz and co-workers, and the isolation of oxidative addition complexes by Ackermann and co-workers.12 This approach has since been extended to include the intermolecular oxidative addition of C─H bonds by chelation assistance13 and with other supporting phosphines.14

While oxidative addition pathways are well-established for C─H activation mediated by iron(0), mechanistic understanding of related reactions with iron(II) remains limited. Beginning with report from Corriu and co-workers on the photochemical cyclometalation of a P(OPh)3 ligand mediated by a (η5-C5H5)Fe(CO)2(silyl) complex, piano stool iron compounds, (η5-C5H5)FeL2X (L = CO, MeCN, NHC or P(OR)3, X = alkyl, aryl, SiR3, or B(OR)2)15-18 have been reported to promote C─H activation of aryl and alkyl groups and computational studies support a redox-neutral, σ-complex assisted metathesis (σ-CAM) pathway.19-21 Klein and co-workers have further applied the directing group strategy with (Me3P)4FeMe2 to the site-selective C─H alkylation of aryl aldimines to furnish octahedral iron(II) products (Scheme 1b).22,23

In addition to cyclopentadienyls and phosphines, other ligands have been shown to support iron(II)-mediated C─H activation.24 Deng and co-workers reported the preparation of isolable, 14-electron (NHC)2FeR2 complexes (NHC = N-heterocyclic carbene; R = alkyl, silyl) which involves a ligand C─H activation,24a while Sunada, Nagashima and co-workers have described indole C(sp2)─H silylation mediated by a six-coordinate disilaferracycle dicarbonyl complex.24b In both reports, C─H activation with iron(II) was proposed to proceed through either a σ-CAM or an Fe(II/IV) redox cycling pathway. Arene C(sp2)─H activation by pincer-supported iron(II) hydrides has been reported independently by Nakajima and Nishibayashi (PNpyrrolideP-supported intermediate-spin iron(II)) and de Ruiter (PCNHCP supported diamagnetic iron(II)) and both invoke a redox-neutral, σ-CAM mechanism.24c,d

While precedented, the mechanistic understanding and applications of iron(II) promoted, redox-neutral C─H functionalization reactions remain underdeveloped. Through a combination of experimental and computational studies, Gutierrez, Neidig, and Ackermann have identified low-spin iron(II)─aryl complexes as post-C─H activation intermediates with arene substrates bearing amide-triazole/quinoline bidentate directing groups.25a-d Analogously, Ribas and co-workers reported an iron(II)-aryl complex supported by a tetradentate N3C macrocyclic ligand as a post-C─H activation intermediate capable of undergoing subsequent C(sp2)─C(sp2) coupling.25e While four-coordinate iron alkyl/aryl complexes were proposed to mediate the C─H cleavage step, the facile C─H activation in these complexes has impeded the isolation of such iron alkyl/aryl intermediates and the investigation of the effects of spin states, coordination geometries and ligand parameters on the reactivity in the C─H activation process remains limited.

Recent results with nickel and cobalt also provide insights for redox-neutral C─H functionalization processes with iron. Ariafard, Canty and Sanford have reported intramolecular C(sp2)─H activation by a putative, cationic Ni(IV) complex (Scheme 1c).26 Our laboratory reported the catalytic directed C─H alkylation of functionalized arenes with bis(phosphine) cobalt complexes.27 Stoichiometric experiments, kinetic data and isotopic labeling supported a cobalt(III) metallacycle that promotes a reversible C─H activation reaction through a redox-neutral σ-CAM pathway.28 Based on these precedents, octahedral, iron(II) d6 complexes were targeted to promote redox neutral C─H functionalization reactions. Here we describe selective C(sp2)─H methylation promoted by iron-(II), d6 complexes (Scheme 1d). A combination of stoichiometric, kinetic and computational studies was used to establish the general features of the iron complex that enable C─H functionalization reactivity.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

### Directed C(sp2)─H Activation and Effect of Ligand Lability and Iron(II) Spin State.

Using a modified protocol from Field and co-workers,29 the bis(phosphine) iron(II) dimethyl complex, (depe)2FeMe2 ( 1 a ) was prepared (see Supporting Information for details). Addition of an excess of pivalophenone 2 a to a benzene-d6 solution of 1 a and heating at 80 °C for 16 h resulted in near quantitative formation of ortho-methylated pivalophenone 3a along with (depe)2Fe(N2) (4), (depe)Fe(η6-pivalophenone) (5a), and free depe ligand (Scheme 2a).30,31 Subjecting independently synthesized 4 to excess 2 a under analogous conditions led to the formation of 5a. While C─H oxidative addition by putative 16-electron bis(phosphine) iron(0) complexes is precedented,11,12 this represents one of the few reports of C─H activation by a well-defined bis(phosphine) iron(II) complex.

Structure–reactivity relationships were explored for the iron-promoted C─H methylation reaction by variation of the phosphine ligand (Scheme 2b). Replacing the depe chelate (cone angle of 115°) with dmpe that has a smaller cone angle of 107° produced no reactivity as (dmpe)2FeMe2 (1b) was inert toward 2 a at both room (23 °C) and elevated (80 °C) temperatures, with no evidence for the consumption of 1b after 16 h.32 Notably, use of monodentate phosphines as in the case of cis-(Me3P)4FeMe2 (1c) and in situ generated cis-PhMe2P)4FeMe2 (1d) resulted in near quantitative methylation of 2 a at ambient temperature. For complex 1c, concurrent formation of the cyclometalated iron hydride was observed, arising from putative C─H activation of remaining 2 a mediated by Fe0(PMe3)4 generated in situ, consistent with reports by Ackermann and co-workers.12 Taken together, these results support the role of ligand lability in promoting C(sp2)─H methylation. With PMe3 and PMe2Ph having a larger cone angle and greater proclivity for dissociation, C─H methylation occurred at ambient temperature while bidentate depe (complex 1 a ) has a higher barrier and requires heating. In addition to cone angle values,33 the dmpe ligand has a smaller buried volume, especially when the secondary coordination sphere is taken into account, than depe (Table S1 and Figure S26, see Supporting Information), and is known to have a higher barrier for dissociation;34 accordingly no C(sp2)─H activation reaction was detected.

Noting the acceleration in rate of C─H activation with the depe-supported iron complex ( 1 a ) over dmpe (1b), iron complexes with other bidentate phosphines with larger P-substituents were studied. Introduction of dcype (cone angle of 142°) resulted in isolation of the tetrahedral, high-spin iron(II) complex, (dcype)FeMe2 (6a) (dcype = 1,2-bis-(dicyclohexylphosphino)ethane; see Supporting Information for synthetic details).35,36 Addition of excess phosphine produced no reaction and no evidence for formation of the corresponding diamagnetic octahedral complexes.36

The reactivity of the four-coordinate iron(II) complex in C(sp2)─H methylation was also evaluated. Addition of an excess of 2 a to benzene-d6 solution of 6a at either ambient temperature or 80 °C produced negligible reaction (Scheme 2b). With in situ generation of the monodentate PEt3 complex (6b) with a relatively large cone angle (132°), trace yields of 3a were observed. These observations establish a significantly high barrier for C(sp2)─H activation by four-coordinate high-spin paramagnetic iron(II) complexes. This likely results from the lack of vacant d orbitals on the high-spin iron(II) center and inhibits substrate coordination.37

### Investigation of Steric and Orbital Effects of X-Type Ligands.

To probe the influence of X-type ligands on the rate and selectivity of the C(sp2)─H methylation reaction, a family of bis(phosphine) iron(II) complexes was synthesized bearing two different hydrocarbyl ligands (Scheme 3a). Treatment of (depe)2FeCl2 with 0.5 equiv of (TMEDA)MgMe2 in diethyl ether and stirring for 1 h at room temperature afforded the iron(II) methyl chloride (8) in 73% isolated yield.38 Addition of 0.5 equiv of the diacetylidomagnesium reagent Mg(C≡CPh)2 to 8 resulted in near quantitative formation of the trans-iron(II) methyl alkynyl complex 9.39 Likewise, arylation of 8 with 0.5 equiv of (TMEDA)Mg(p-tolyl)2 followed by filtration and recrystallization in diethyl ether at −35 °C afforded red-orange crystals in 85% yield. The identity of product was confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD) as trans-(depe)2FeMe(4-tolyl) (10) with an idealized octahedral geometry. Observation of a singlet at 84.7 ppm in the benzene-d6 31P{1H} NMR spectrum confirmed exclusive formation of the trans isomer of 10. Attempts to prepare (depe)2Fe(4-tolyl)R complexes with R = ethyl, benzyl, CH2SiMe3 following an analogous route were unsuccessful (see the Supporting Information).

The rate of C─H activation also varied as a function of the identity of the X-type ligand (Scheme 3c). For (depe)2FeMe2 ( 1 a ), ortho-C(sp2)─H methylation of 2 a was not observed at ambient temperature after 16 h and heating to 80 °C was required. In contrast, complex 10 (where X = 4-tolyl) yielded near quantitative conversion to the methylated product 3a (97% NMR yield) at room temperature after 16 h, similar to the reactivity of 1c, albeit with 10 being more thermally stable and more straightforward to handle. This supports the role of steric effects where phosphine arm dissociation is favored by a larger X-type ligand (A-value, p-tolyl ~3.0).40 Consistent with this proposal is the lack of C─H activation observed for the iron(II) methyl chloride complex 8 with a less sterically demanding X-type ligand (A-value, Cl = 0.43–0.53).40 Subjecting the iron(II) methyl alkynyl complex 9 (A-value, alkynyl = 0.41–0.52)40 to identical reaction conditions produced negligible consumption of 9 or detection of any C─C coupled product at both 23 and 80 °C. While the Fe─Me bond in 1 a and 10 is more basic (pKa of methane ~50) than the Fe─Ar bond in 10 (pKa of Ar─H ~ 43), the latter promotes more rapid C─H activation, demonstrating that the pKa of the X-type ligand does not have a significant impact on the rate of iron(II)-mediated C─H activation.

Comparison of the reactivity of 1 a , 9 10 establishes the combined influence of the size and orbital hybridization of X-type ligands on the rate of C─H methylation. The ortho methylation of 2 a mediated by analogous complexes of the form (depe)2FeMe(4-R-C6H4) (R = H, OMe, NMe2, Figure S23, see Supporting Information) was also studied and comparable yields of ortho-methylated product 3a and similarly exclusive formation of the C(sp2)─CH3 coupled product were obtained (Scheme S1, see Supporting Information). Together with the observed effect of phosphine ligand lability, these findings are consistent with a mechanism involving phosphine dissociation prior to substrate coordination and C─H activation.

### Effect of Directing Group Identity on C(sp2)─H Methylation.

The chemoselectivity of C(sp2)─H activation and C(sp2)─C coupling mediated by complex 10 was explored with a host of directing groups (Scheme 4a). Systematic variation of the ketone substituents from tert-butyl to methyl ( 2 a –d) furnished the ortho C(sp2)─H methylation products (3a–d) in good to high yields ranging from 68 to 81%. The trifluoromethylated variant, 3e was also tolerated although a diminished yield of 34% was obtained. Aryl aldehydes were also tolerated in the iron-promoted C(sp2)─H methylation reaction as use of 2e provided the desired product 3e in 49% yield. These data suggest that the size of the directing group and the presence of moderately acidic α-to-carbonyl protons have limited impact on C(sp2)─H methylation reactivity.

Arylcarbonyl directing groups (2g and 2h) were also effective and ortho C(sp2)─H methylation products were obtained in high yields of 85–91%. For the electronically differentiated benzophenone 2h, selective C(sp2)─H methylation was observed on aryl ring containing the methoxy group meta to the site of C─H methylation (3h/3h′ = 80:20). Analogous regioselective directed C─H methylation mediated by complex 1c has been reported by Li and co-workers for unsymmetrical diaryl imines,22d implying a potentially generic preference of iron(II)-mediated redox-neutral C─H activation at the more electron-deficient site.

For carbonyl substrates 2 a –i, exclusive formation of the ortho C(sp2)─H methylation product was observed with no evidence for C(sp2)─C(sp2) coupling. This further corroborates the observed trend in chemoselectivity where the Fe─CAr bond in 10 mediates selective C(sp2)─H activation while the Fe─CMe bond is involved in C─C reductive elimination.

With nitrogen-containing directing groups, C─H cleavage remained facile but the subsequent C─C reductive elimination was impeded (Scheme 4b). For example, addition of 10 equiv of benzo[h]quinoline (2i) to a benzene-d6 solution containing one equivalent of 10 at ambient temperature produced a color change to deep purple after 6 h concomitant with complete consumption of 10 and quantitative formation of toluene. Isomers of the cyclometalated iron methyl aryl complex containing a κ1-coordinating bis(phosphine) were observed by 1H and 31P NMR spectroscopy (Figure S24, see Supporting Information), analogous to the reactivity of complex 1c reported by Klein and co-workers.41 Similar reactivity was observed with imine directing groups (2j and 2k). Formation of the C─H methylation product was not observed at room temperature and heating to 80 °C or oxidation to iron(III) was required to induce C─C reductive elimination (Figure S25, see Supporting Information).42

With ester (2l), amide (2m) or sulfonamide (2n) directing groups, sluggish C─H activation reactivity was observed (Scheme 4c). Treatment of one equivalent of 10 with 10 equiv of 2l, 2m, or 2n separately in benzene-d6 did not result in an observable color change and no evidence for consumption of 10 or formation of the ortho-methylated product was obtained (at either 23 or 80 °C), by 1H and 31P NMR spectroscopy.

### Mechanistic Experiments.

To rationalize the observed trends in iron(II)-mediated C─H activation and to gain mechanistic insight, kinetic studies and deuterium labeling experiments were conducted. The visual time normalization analysis (VTNA) developed by Burés and co-workers was applied to the reaction between 1 a and 2 a at 80 °C (Scheme 5a(i)).43 By varying the concentration of the pivalophenone, a first-order dependence on 2 a was observed (Scheme 5a(ii)). Addition of excess depe ligand inhibited the formation of 3a and an inverse first order dependence was measured (Scheme 5a(iii)). Taken together, the experimental rate law (eq 1) supports a pathway involving initial dissociation of the phosphine followed by rate-determining C─H activation.

$$ (1) rate = k [ 2 a ] 1 [ 1 a ] 1 [ depe ] − 1 $$

To gain insight into the rate-determining step, deuterium kinetic isotope effect (KIE) experiments were carried out (Scheme 5b). In separate J. Young NMR tubes, six equivalents of 2 a or 2 a -d5 were added to a benzene-d6 solution of 1 a and heated to 80 °C. Monitoring the time course of the reaction by 1H NMR spectroscopy provided a k H ∕ k D value of 2.2(1), supporting C─H cleavage in the rate-determining step (Scheme 5b(i)). When 2 a -d5 was added, the formation of CH3D was also observed. An intermolecular competition deuterium KIE experiment was performed with a benzene-d6 solution of 1a subjected to an equimolar mixture of 2 a and 2 a -d5 (Scheme 5b(ii)). The reaction was stopped at 10% conversion, and the ratio of products (3a and 3a-d4) determined by 1H NMR spectroscopy produced a k H ∕ k D of 2.9(2) at 80 °C, with no evidence for H/D exchange in the recovered substrate(s). Treatment of pivalophenone 2 a with independently synthesized iron di(trideuteromethyl) complex 1 a -d6 under analogous reaction conditions (Scheme 5c) resulted in near quantitative formation of the trideuteromethylated product 3a-d3 and trideuteromethane (CD3H). These observations corroborate C─H activation as irreversible and rate-determining.

### Proposed Mechanism.

From the combined results of the stoichiometric studies, rate law determination, and KIE experiments, a mechanism for C─H methylation of pivalophenone 2a mediated by bis(phosphine) iron complexes is proposed (Scheme 6). Reversible dissociation of one arm of the bis(phosphine) ligand from the six-coordinate, 18-electron (depe)2FeMeX generates a vacant coordination site for substrate coordination forming the intermediate, Int1. Complete dissociation of the dangling κ1-bis(phosphine) opens a second coordination site for the formation of the putative C(sp2)─H σ-complex (Int2). It is unlikely that complete dissociation of one bis(phosphine) to generate a four-coordinate Int1′ precedes substrate coordination as the four-coordinate, high-spin iron(II) dimethyl complex (6a) was unreactive for C─H activation (Scheme 2b).

From Int2, rate-determining C─H activation likely occurs through a redox-neutral σ-bond metathesis (σ-CAM) pathway (see computational studies in Figure 1). In bis(phosphine) iron(II) complexes bearing different X-type ligands, an orbital hybridization effect is observed where C─H activation by the Fe─X bond with a larger partial s-character is preferred. Dissociation of the C─H activation byproduct (HX) from the resultant σ-complex (Int3) generates a five-coordinate iron(II) complex, Int4, which then undergoes C(sp2)─C(sp3) reductive elimination to generate the ortho-methylated product 3. The iron products are either the bis(phosphine) iron(0) dinitrogen or (η6-arene) complexes that form in the presence of N2 or excess 2 a .

### Density Functional Theory Studies.

Computational studies were conducted to gain more detailed insights in the pathway for C─H activation and to account for the observed chemoselectivity. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed for the singlet, triplet, and quintet potential energy surfaces (PES). Geometries of all ground and transition states were optimized using the TPSS functional and the Karlsruhe def2-SVP basis set.44,45 Single-point calculations were performed using the TPSSh functional with a def2-TZVPP basis set due to its reported accuracy in the prediction of spin-state energies of first-row transition metal complexes.46 The calculated geometry and lowest spin states of 1 a , 10 and 4 are consistent with experimental observations obtained from single-crystal X-ray diffraction and 1H and 31P NMR spectroscopy.

For ortho C─H methylation of 2 a mediated by the trans isomer of 1 a (Figure 1a), the reaction commences on the singlet surface where displacement of one phosphine of the depe ligand by 2 a is reversible and endergonic ΔG° = +32.5 kcal/mol), furnishing the corresponding iron substrate complex, 1[Int1]. Rate-determining C─H cleavage occurs with a barrier of 35.4 kcal/mol (relative to [ 1 a ] 1 ) and proceeds on the singlet surface through a transition state (1[TS1]) consistent with those established for σ-CAM reactions.47 Attempts to locate alternative transition states for concerted C─H oxidative addition converged to 1[TS1]. The calculations support formation of a C(sp2)─H agostic complex with the low-spin iron(II) center in 1[Int1] with d(Fe─H) = 1.637 Å. On the potential energy surfaces with higher spin-states, significantly weaker agostic interactions were observed with d(Fe─H) = 2.960 and 2.384 Å for 3[Int1] and 5[Int1], respectively (Table S4, see Supporting Information). Moreover, partial C(sp2)─H bond cleavage is observed on the singlet PES with the C(sp2)─H bond (1.166 Å) in 1[Int1] significantly lengthened relative to that in 3[Int1] and 5[Int1] (1.089 and 1.091 Å, respectively). The greater propensity of the low-spin iron(II) center for forming stronger C─H agostic interactions lowers the activation barrier for C─H activation prior to the transition state.

The resulting six-coordinate iron(II) alkane complex, η2-(H─CH3) (Int2) generated from C─H cleavage has a triplet ground state 3[Int2] with a thermally accessible singlet first excited state 1[Int2] (2.4 kcal/mol above 3[Int2]). On the triplet surface, methane dissociation from the iron(II) center then yields the five-coordinate iron(II) methyl κ2-C,O-phenonyl intermediate 3[Int3]. Subsequent C─C reductive coupling occurs through a low-lying triplet transition state 3[TS2] to afford Int4, with a much lower barrier of 16.3 kcal/mol (relative to 3[Int3]) than the C─H activation step (35.4 kcal/mol). C─C bond formation on the singlet (1[TS2]) and quintet (5[TS2]) surfaces incurs significantly higher barriers (15.2 and 13.1 kcal/mol higher than 3[TS2]).47,48 Ligand substitution of the ortho-methylated pivalophenone 3a with dinitrogen and the depe ligand resulted in the irreversible formation of the experimentally observed (depe)2Fe(N2) complex (4) with a highly exergonic ΔG° (−41.7 kcal/mol relative to 1[Int4]).

By comparison, computations on the cis isomer of complex 1a, similarly suggest C─H activation on the singlet surface as the rate-determining step, with comparable barriers of 34.4 and 35.2 kcal/mol for the two possible configurations (Figure S37, see Supporting Information). This is consistent with the observation of a largely unchanged cis/trans ratio of 1a during the course of the methylation reaction (Figure S33, see Supporting Information). It is noted that the computed barriers (34.4–35.4 kcal/mol) are slightly higher than expected (~30 kcal/mol) based on the experimental observations, which may be an artifact of the chosen DFT functional.

To gain a better understanding of the observed chemoselectivity in C─H activation and C─C coupling, the C─H functionalization of 2 a with (depe)2FeMe(4-tolyl) (10) was computationally investigated (Figure 1b). Analogous to 1 a , a reversible and energetically uphill ligand substitution of the depe ligand for the pivalophenone ( 2 a ) generates the substrate chelate 1[Int5] with a slightly lower-lying triplet state 3[Int5] (by −1.4 kcal/mol).

The subsequent C─H activation was found to be both rate- and selectivity-determining, proceeding through σ-CAM transition states on the singlet surface (1[TS3] and 1[TS4]). C(sp2)─H cleavage assisted by the tolyl ligand in 1[TS3] incurs a lower barrier (ΔΔG‡ = 2.1 kcal/mol) than 1[TS4] where the Fe─C(sp3) bond is involved. This corresponds to a 35:1 selectivity, consistent with the experimental observation of the exclusive formation of the C(sp2)─C(sp3) coupled product 3a. The observed selectivity is intriguing considering that the Fe─Caryl bond is calculated to be significantly stronger (BDFcalc = 48.1 kcal/mol) than the Fe─Cmethyl with BDFEcalc = 30.5 kcal/mol (Scheme S2, see Supporting Information). Analysis of the geometries of 1[TS3] and 1[TS4] shows similar four-centered transition structures (Figure 1c). A shorter Fe···H distance in 1[TS3] (1.518 Å) versus in 1[TS4] (1.532 Å) suggests a greater stabilization of the former by a stronger partial Fe─H bonding interaction,49 which is consistent with the observed selectivity for the tolyl ligand as the preferred H atom acceptor in the C─H cleavage step.

Analogous to the calculated PES for 1 a , after a spin crossover event, C─C reductive coupling likely proceeds through triplet transition states with significantly lower barriers than the respective C─H activation steps (Figure S36, see Supporting Information). These results further support C─H activation as the rate- and selectivity-determining step in the C─H functionalization mediated by bis(phosphine) iron(II) complexes with different X-type ligands.

### Summarizing the General Principles for Iron(II)-Mediated C─H Methylation.

Combining the experimental and computational results obtained for the structure–activity relationship of bis(phosphine) iron(II) complexes in directed C(sp2)─H methylation, general principles for enabling iron(II) complexes to achieve facile, redox neutral C─H functionalization have been established and are illustrated in Figure 2.

### Effect of Ligand Lability.

The relative size of both L-(Scheme 2b) and X-type (Scheme 3c) ligands was found to determine the rate of iron(II) mediated C—H activation by controlling ligand lability and the equilibrium position for ligand dissociation prior to the rate-determining C—H activation (Figure 1a). Experimental and computational studies support ground-state destabilization due to a more significant steric penalty between larger L- and X-type ligands, which increases the lability of L-type ligands to favor substrate coordination, thus accelerating overall C—H activation. By comparison, with iron(II) complexes containing sterically attenuated L-type (e.g., dmpe in 1b, Scheme 2b) and X-type ligands (e.g., chloro in 8 and alkynyl in 9, Scheme 3c), the lack of sufficient steric interactions in the ground state results in decreased ligand lability and a higher barrier for phosphine dissociation, accounting for the observed lack of C—H activation. Changing the denticity of L-type ligands from bi- to monodentate leads to rate acceleration as exemplified by PMe3 and PMe2Ph, consistent with the well-established chelate effect.50 It should also be noted that the positive correlation between L-type ligand sterics as measured by Tolman’s cone angle (dmpe < depe < PMe3 < PMe2Ph) and iron(II) C—H methylation reactivity (1b < 1a < 1c ≈ 1d) is only valid within a certain cone angle range (approximately 107—122° in this system) that permits the formation of octahedral diamagnetic iron(II) complexes.

While effects of the size of L-type ligands on ligand lability have been invoked in the cis-trans isomerization of phosphine metal complexes by phosphine dissociation,22b,29,51 the effect of ligand sterics on the redox-neutral C—H activation reactivity of late transition-metal complexes has rarely been explored or demonstrated. Beginning with a well-defined bis(phosphine) iron(II) complex, this study represents a rare case where the steric interactions between L- and X-type ligands as a key determinant of the rate of ligand dissociation were determined and correlated with the rate of redox-neutral C—H activation mediated by first-row transition metals.

### Effect of Metal Spin State.

The stark contrast in reactivity of high-spin paramagnetic 4-coordinate iron(II) complexes versus the low-spin diamagnetic 6-coordinate counterparts (Scheme 2b) suggests the preference for a low spin state in iron(II)-mediated redox-neutral C—H activation. Specifically, reversible phosphine dissociation from the low-spin iron(II) center (Scheme 5a(iii) and Figure 1a) forms a five-coordinate diamagnetic (κ2-depe)(κ1-depe)Fe(II) complex, where substrate coordination is spin-allowed and initiates C─H bond cleavage.

It is worth noting that changes in spin state of the iron(II) center are determined by the size of the L-type ligands. Comparison across various phosphine ligands (dmpe, depe, PMe3, PMe2Ph, PEt3, dcype) with similar electronic properties (as measured by TEP in Scheme 2b) and varying steric properties (based on well-established cone angles) indicates the presence of a threshold cone angle value between 122 and 132° that divides the iron dimethyl complexes between being low-spin diamagnetic and high-spin paramagnetic. For larger phosphine ligands with cone angles greater than 132°, the decrease in coordination number around the iron(II) center due to the space constraint in its surrounding coordination sphere induces a spin change in the ground state, drastically altering its reactivity. This marks a fundamental departure in the design principles for C—H activation at iron versus its palladium and nickel counterparts. For Pd and Ni, a low-spin diamagnetic ground state is still preferred with a decrease in coordination number, and at-metal C—H activation is accelerated due to less steric demand for substrate coordination.52 In comparison, the access to higher spin states means that a decrease in coordination number will not necessarily enhance C—H activation reactivity of Fe complexes.

In the current literature on iron(II)-mediated redox-neutral C—H activation, the understanding of the spin state and coordination environment of the iron center is limited to computational studies.13a,15,17,18,22,24,25 Beginning with well-defined low- and high-spin iron(II) methyl complexes, the results described here represent the first combined empirical and theoretical investigation of the effect of iron(II) spin state on the rate of redox-neutral C—H activation. For example, while high-spin four-coordinate iron(II) complexes have been hypothesized as pre-C—H activation intermediates,25c this study suggests that these complexes are unlikely to be directly involved in the C—H activation step. Demonstrating that rate-determining C—H activation (Scheme 5 and Figure 1) preferentially traversing through a singlet transition state provides experimental validation for the computational studies by Ackermann and Chen.25d,47

### Effect of Orbital Hybridization on Chemoselectivity.

Based on the experimental evidence (Scheme 3b) and computational investigations (Figure 1b), an orbital effect on the chemo-selectivity of the rate-determining C—H activation step (Figure 2) was established using isolated (depe)2Fe(II) complexes bearing different X-type ligands. Specifically, the hybridization of the X-type ligands controls the kinetic selectivity of the C—H activation (and subsequent C—C coupling): despite being stronger than the Fe─Cmethyl bond, the Fe─Caryl bond preferentially participates in the four-centered σ-CAM transition state, due to a lower reorganization energy for the less directional molecular orbital with a higher partial s-character.

While effect of orbital hybridization on chemoselectivity has been established for σ-bond metathesis mediated by d0 early transition metals and lanthanides,53 few studies have established the feasibility of analogous principles for σ-CAM, which differs from the former in terms of transition state features including partial M─H bonding interactions and is typically mediated by dn>0 transition metals.54 By comparison, the results reported in this study not only establish that the effect of orbital hybridization on the relative rate of σ-bond metathesis is also applicable to σ-CAM pathways, but also experimentally demonstrate how such orbital effects are utilized to impart chemoselectivity to C─H bond activation.

### Effect of Directing Groups.

Based on the yields of the C(sp2)—H methylation reaction mediated by 10 (Scheme 4), comparison of various ketone/aldehyde directing groups demonstrates no significant impact on the reactivity when the size of the substituents on the directing group was varied or when mildly acidic α-to-carbonyl protons were present. The latter suggests that C(sp2)—H activation outcompetes α-to-carbonyl C(sp3)—H deprotonation. The presence of C(sp3)─F bonds in the directing group, however, diminishes the yield of C(sp2)—H activation, a result of thermodynamically favorable iron fluoride formation or a less-donating carbonyl ligand.55

With more strongly σ-donating N(sp2) directing groups in imine and pyridine derivatives, the singlet state was stabilized and C—H activation remains facile. The resulting six-coordinate product has a high barrier for C—C reductive elimination, resulting in the formation of stable diamagnetic cyclometalated iron complexes. The stronger coordinating ability of N(sp2) directing group disfavors dissociation from the iron(II) center to access the requisite five-coordinate intermediate to promote reductive elimination. This is corroborated by similar observations made with imines by Klein41 and with bidentate amide-triazole and amide-quinoline directing groups studied by Neidig, Gutierrez and Ackermann.24a-d

With ester, amide and sulfonamide directing groups, the sluggish C—H activation is attributed to less favorable coordination of these directing groups to the iron(II) center. It is hypothesized that the sp2 oxygen lone pairs in these directing groups are less coordinating due to the inductive electron-withdrawing effect of the nearby electronegative atoms.

Overall, comparing the C—H methylation reactivity among different directing groups suggests that the carbonyl directing group in ketones and aldehydes is optimal for iron(II)-mediated redox-neutral C—H activation due to a balancing of σ-coordination ability which is needed to promote the directed C—H activation but not sufficiently coordinating to inhibit dissociation to access the requisite five-coordinate intermediate required for reductive elimination.

## CONCLUSIONS

General principles for enabling iron(II) complexes to promote efficient redox-neutral C—H activation and methylation reactions were established based on a combination of stoichiometric reactivity, mechanistic experiments, and computational studies of directed arene C—H activation. With six-coordinate bis(bidentate phosphine) iron(II) complexes, more rapid C—H activation was observed when ligand lability was enhanced by an increase in ligand sterics or a reduction in L-type ligand denticity. Computational studies established the preference for low-spin iron(II) complexes for the cleavage of the C(sp2)─H bond. The effect of arene directing groups was also systematically explored with a demonstrated preference for ketone and aldehyde directing groups with tolerance of varying sterics as well as the presence of acidic α-hydrogens. Furthermore, exclusive chemoselectivity in the C—H activation and C—C coupling was achieved by exploiting the effect of orbital hybridization of X-type ligands. Kinetic and deuterium labeling experiments and computational studies support a reversible ligand dissociation followed by a rate-determining C—H activation featuring a four-membered, singlet σ-CAM transition state, thus providing the mechanistic rationale for the observed general principles. Notably, this study serves as a foundational example of experimental and theoretical elucidation of the orbital hybridization effect in σ-bond metathesis (σ-CAM) mediated by dn>0 transition metals. Overall, the general principles from this study will improve the understanding of the key factors for the future development of transition metal systems for facile and selective chemical bond activation.

## Abstract

This paper introduces a reconfigurable underwater robot system, RS-ModCubes, which allows scalable multi-robot configuration. An RS-ModCubes system consists of multiple ModCube modules, that can travel underwater with 6 DoFs and assemble with each other into a larger structure with onboard electromagnets. This system is designed to support diverse underwater applications through modularity and reconfigurability, eliminating the need to customize mechanical designs for a specific task. We present a modeling framework tailored for such reconfigurable robot systems, with hydrodynamics integrated based on Monte Carlo approximation. A model-based feedforward PD (PD) controller serves as the baseline for control. Inspired by dexterous manipulation, we evaluated the robot’s maximum task wrench space and power efficiency, compared against four commercial underwater robots. RS-ModCubes is validated via both real-world experiments and simulations, including individual and multi-module trajectory tracking and hovering docking. We open-source the design and code to facilitate future research: https://jiaxi-zheng.github.io/ModCube.github.io/.

## I Introduction

Underwater robots allow us to explore the vast benthic world, even reaching the deepest regions of the ocean, such as the Mariana Trench. However, these robots are often costly to build and limited to their designed tasks: The configuration of an underwater robot is typically specific to its designated application and does not generalize to other tasks. Such task-specific designs require extensive customization, raising costs and limiting their utility across diverse operations, which presents significant barriers to widespread adoption in research and commercial settings.

To address these limitations, we introduce a low-cost modular robot platform, RS-ModCubes. RS-ModCubes’ design features omnidirectional mobility, and multiple modules, ModCube, can be reconfigured into various configurations and shapes. In the related study, such robots are often termed as MSRR [1]. In this work, our objective is to take advantage of the modularity and reconfigurability of RS-ModCubes for practical applications, including underwater inspection, environmental monitoring, and search and rescue.

ModCube robots (Section III) are designed with symmetric structure to travel in harsh underwater environments with 6 DoF. We developed a MDS (MDS) to support modular docking and operate full-body planning and navigation tasks. The modular design allows adaptation to different tasks that require different robot structures or under different space limitations.

We model the floating-base system dynamics of ModCube and RS-ModCubes in Lagrangian form (Section IV and V). A critical challenge lies in characterizing hydrodynamics due to morphing nature of RS-ModCubes. We use Monte Carlo method to approximate frontal area values and store directional drag forces in a Lookup Table for efficient retrieval. A model-based PD controller is implemented for state control.

We propose a novel characterization and visualization method (Section VI-B) inspired by dexterous manipulation to quantify the capabilities of underwater robots. This method evaluates task space as determined by actuator allocation, using metrics such as Willmore energy and Dirichlet energy to assess workspace continuity and smoothness. These insights guide optimal configuration selection for future complex reconfigurations.
