This work lays a methodological groundwork for system modeling, control strategies, and the analysis of trade-offs in actuation, configuration, and power allocation, serving as a basis for future scaling efforts. We demonstrate trajectory tracking for ModCube and RS-ModCubes through a series of real-world and simulation experiments (Section VII), along with reconfiguration experiments involving two ModCube modules.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- 1. The design details of the ModCube and RS-ModCubes system.

- 2. A modeling framework for individual ModCube and RS-ModCubes dynamics.

- 3. A structured characterization method that quantifies and visualizes robot morphological performance.

- 4. Experimental validation in water tanks, demonstrating the feasibility of the design and modeling framework in the real world.

## II Related Work

### II-A Configuration Setup of Underwater Robots

Underwater robot designs vary widely based on task requirements. Full-size ROV are effective for operations but suffer from limited mobility due to their large size [2]. Compact ROV, typically box-shaped with five to eight thrusters, such as those in our previous work [3] [4], enable omnidirectional maneuverability, but exhibit poor hydrodynamic performance. For long-range missions, torpedo-shaped robots [5] offer streamlined efficiency. In summary, today’s underwater robots are primarily designed for a single purpose that does not generalize to different tasks.

In this paper, we present ModCube, a modular robotic platform, and the box-shape designed for ease of manufacturing. ModCube is equipped with eight thrusters arranged in two groups of four: four thrusters are vertically inclined at 45 degrees, with a similar configuration applied horizontally. Building on our earlier work [3], this design enables omnidirectional mobility, positioning ModCube as a versatile solution for a wide range of underwater tasks.

### II-B Modular Robotic Swarms

Swarm robotic systems exhibit versatility across diverse environments and applications. We categorize their capabilities into three primary types:

#### II-B1 Shape Reconfiguration

Shape reconfiguration involves transitioning from individual modules to a joint configuration or modifying an existing configuration. Ground-based systems such as SMORES-EP [6] and multi-legged robots [7] showcase adaptability to varying terrains. M-Blocks [8] focus on momentum-driven actuation for reconfiguration. In aerial domains, platforms like Modquad [9] achieve stable operations through self-assembly.

#### II-B2 Collaborative Construction

Collaborative construction involves discrete modules working together to build larger, programmable structures. Reprogrammable robots [10], for example, create lattice structures for adaptive infrastructure, while termite-inspired robots [11] enable autonomous assembly through low-level individual actions that lead to collective high-level outcomes.

#### II-B3 Formation Tasks without Interaction

This category encompasses swarms that operate without direct interaction between modules. Examples include distributed force control methods [12], where modules collaborate indirectly. Fish-inspired swarm systems [13] focus on bio-behavioral exploration, prioritizing collective behavior over task adaptability or reconfiguration.

### II-C Underwater Reconfigurable Modular Robots

Underwater Reconfigurable robots can be classified into passive and active reconfiguration systems.

#### II-C1 Passive Reconfiguration

Passive reconfiguration systems rely on human-in-the-loop assembly [14], restricting their adaptivity in complex environments. Examples include bio-inspired designs like Soft Robotic Fish (SoFi) [15] and heterogeneous modular cubic robots [16], which lack integrated capabilities for navigation, planning, and perception.

#### II-C2 Active Reconfiguration

Active underwater self-reconfiguration systems are scarce due to the nascent nature of the field and the significant challenges associated with control, modeling, and conducting swarm hardware experiments underwater. The work [17] lacks advanced high-end capabilities. An energy-heuristic strategy for self-reconfiguration was proposed in [18], but its practical implementation remains largely unvalidated.

## III ModCube Design

### III-A System Overview

#### III-A1 Onboard Computation

Each ModCube can optionally integrate an Nvidia Jetson NX for onboard perception, planning, and control, enabling a full-stack robotics pipeline without tethering. Alternatively, a ground-based computer can enable these tasks via tethered communication.

#### III-A2 Electronics Layout

We organize electronic components into 3 layers to optimize cabin space for electronics following a bottom-up design strategy (* denote optional components):

- • Bottom layer: Electric relay, Battery*, ESC (ESC),

- • Middle layer: MCU (MCU), Onboard Computer*, Power Distribution Board,

- • Top layer: USB Camera*

#### III-A3 Dual Power Supply

ModCube supports both external power supply and onboard power supply by equipping batteries, offering flexibility in operational scenarios depending on experiment or deployment requirements.

#### III-A4 Cost Efficiency

Each ModCube is priced at approximately $800 (excluding the onboard computer), with customized thrusters costing $14 each and delivering a maximum thrust of 10 N. This design representing a cost-effective solution compared to high-end commercial systems, as illustrated in Fig. 5 D–G.

#### III-A5 Modularity and Fabrication

The modular design enables ModCube to accommodate up to six docking disks. For visualization, Fig. 2(B) depicts a configuration with four docking disks, while the experiments in Fig. 6 and Fig. 7 simplify this setup by using only two disks.

The ModCube features a dual-layer shell architecture: The inner layer consists of a metal frame, providing structural support, while the outer layer offers collision protection and serves as a modular attachment interface for components such as docking disks, manipulators, DVL (DVL), which measures the velocity of the vehicle relative to the sea bottom, or scanning sonars.

The outer layer and thruster cowling are fabricated from 3D-printed nylon PA12, coated with waterproof paint, allowing operation at depths of up to 50 m. Thruster propellers are 3D-printed from aluminum, and the cowlings, with a diameter of 56 mm, enclose waterproof brushless motors. The watertight housing consists of an acrylic cylindrical body with an aluminum flange for secure cable connections.

### III-B Magnetic Docking System

A high-tolerance docking mechanism is critical for enabling robots to dock and detach smoothly during self-assembly. We adopt MDS design [19], where an electronic relay controls the power state of the electromagnet, facilitating docking and detachment. The docking mechanism incorporates two disk types: Probe and Drogue, as shown in Fig. 2(B). Each disk features a circular arrangement of convex pins and concave notches in an alternating pattern, visible from a side projection. This design ensures secure interlocking and prevents relative rotation between the Probe and Drogue disks in the docked state. Additionally, a guidance rail is integrated into the docking disk to provide a positioning tolerance of 4 mm and a rotational tolerance of 50 degrees. The docking disks are fabricated using Photopolymer Resin material.

## IV ModCube: Model and Control

### IV-A ModCube Dynamics

Following Fossen’s formulation [20], the general dynamics of underwater robots are expressed in matrix vector notation. Position and orientation are represented by $\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$ in World-fixed frame $\{\mathcal{W}\}$ . Velocity is represented by $\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$ in body-fixed frame $\{\mathcal{B}\}$ . The kinematic relationship is:

$$ \dot{\boldsymbol{\eta}}=J(\boldsymbol{\eta})\boldsymbol{\nu} $$

where $J(\boldsymbol{\eta})$ is the Jacobian matrix for the kinematic transformation. The single ModCube’s dynamic model expressed in $\{\mathcal{B}\}$ is given by:

$$ \mathbf{M}\dot{\boldsymbol{\nu}}+\mathbf{C}(\boldsymbol{\nu})\boldsymbol{\nu}+\boldsymbol{D}_{lut}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{v}_{r}})\boldsymbol{\mathbf{v}_{r}}+\mathbf{g}(\boldsymbol{\eta})=\boldsymbol{\tau} $$

where $\mathbf{M}$ is the combined mass matrix including rigid body $\mathbf{M}_{RB}$ and added mass effect $\mathbf{M}_{A}$ . $\mathbf{C}(\boldsymbol{\nu})$ accounts for Coriolis and centrifugal forces. $\boldsymbol{D}_{lut}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{v}_{r}})$ denotes the drag force retrieved from lookup table defined in Algorithm 1. $\mathbf{g}({\boldsymbol{\eta}})$ includes buoyancy and gravitational forces designed to be zero. The wrench generated by the actuators is represented by $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ . $\mathbf{v}_{r}$ is the relative velocity between the robot and the surrounding fluid field.

### IV-B ModCube Control

Model-based PD controller with feed-forward compensation can be written as:

$$ \boldsymbol{\tau}=K_{P}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}+K_{D}\dot{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}}+\mathbf{M}\dot{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{d}+\mathbf{C}({\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{m}){\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{m}+\boldsymbol{D}_{lut}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{v}_{r}})\boldsymbol{\mathbf{v}_{r}} $$

where, $K_{P}$ and $K_{D}$ represent the proportional and derivative gains respectively. $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$ denotes the position and orientation error. ${\boldsymbol{\nu}_{d}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{m}$ are desired velocity and measured velocity in $\{\mathcal{W}\}$ .

Relationship between control input $u$ and power consumption $P$ of thruster is modeled using polynomial functions:

$$ P(f)=c_{f}\boldsymbol{\zeta}(f(u)),\quad f(u)=c_{u}\boldsymbol{\zeta}(u) $$

where, $f(u)$ is the thrust force. $\boldsymbol{\zeta}(x)=[1,x,x^{2},\ldots,x^{5}]^{T}$ represents the vector of polynomial basis functions, while $c_{f}$ and $c_{u}$ denote the polynomial parameter matrices. The overall force and moment exerted on the vehicle are calculated as follows:

$$ {{J_{t}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left[\begin{matrix}p_{i}^{t}\\
r_{i}^{t}\times p_{i}^{t}\end{matrix}\right],\quad F_{T}={J_{t}}^{+}\boldsymbol{\tau}} $$

where $\boldsymbol{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$ is the applied wrench from Eq. 2, ${\quad F_{T}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{t}\times 1}$ is the thrust matrix ( $n_{t}$ is the total number of the thruster), and ${J_{t}}$ is Jacobian matrix mapping joint space to work space, ${J_{t}}^{+}$ is the pseudo-inverse of ${J_{t}}$ . ### IV-D ModCube Hydrodynamics

In fluid environments, the shape of locomotors vary over time, leading to variations in drag forces [21]. Accurately modeling these dynamic changes is crucial for understanding and predicting the behavior of shape-varying. The drag force ${F}_{\text{drag}}\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$ is given by:

$$ {F}_{\text{drag}}(\mathbf{v}_{r})=-\frac{1}{2}\rho C_{d}A\|\mathbf{v}_{r}\|\mathbf{v}_{r}, $$

where $C_{d}$ is the drag coefficient, computed via CFD in Ansys Fluent with $\{\|\mathbf{v}_{r}\|=1\,\text{m/s}\mid\{\mathcal{B}\}\}$ , and $\rho$ is the fluid density. The frontal area $A$ , orthogonal to the velocity vector, is approximated in Algorithm 1. $\mathbf{v}_{r}$ denotes the relative velocity of the robot with respect to the fluid, ensuring $\{{F}_{\text{drag}}/\|{F}_{\text{drag}}\|=\mathbf{v}_{r}/\|\mathbf{v}_{r}\|\}$ .

The mid graph in Fig. 3 visualizes the approximated drag spaces $\boldsymbol{D}_{lut}$ for three distinct RS-ModCubes configurations. Calculated drag forces ${F}_{\text{drag}}$ are compared with CFD results for an individual ModCube, shown in Fig. 3 (I) in the bottom graph. The comparison spans seven flow directions, indicated on the x-axis. Notable deviations in the (1,1,1) direction are attributed to sharper leading edges, which streamline the flow, reduce turbulent wake formation, and consequently lower drag forces.

## V RS-ModCubes: Model and Control

### V-A RS-ModCubes Connectivity Analysis

Two conditions are used to determine ifdocking between ModCube modules is successful. If both conditions are satisfied, the docking is considered successful:

(1) Condition 1: the current over the electromagnet exceeds a threshold of $\pm 70\,\text{mA}$ . The threshold is suggested by the data collected from over ten real-robot docking experiments, as discussed in Section VII-C and visualized in Fig. 7. (2) Condition 2: the relative position between two modules equals the length of one ModCube and stabilizes.

### V-B Proximity Effects of the Docking Process

We assume docked RS-ModCubes introduce jet interference, potentially affecting system dynamics. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted experiments to measure the one-directional force tracking for an individual ModCube and a two-module RS-ModCubes configuration, as shown in Fig. 4. The percentage difference between two tracking results’ RMSE is 0.46%, thus we consider the interference caused by docking to be negligible.

### V-C RS-ModCubes Modeling

The mass distribution and inertia of each add-on module in RS-ModCubes vary significantly, introducing notable changes to the system dynamics. The total mass $\mathbf{M}_{rsm}$ and position of CoM $\mathbf{r_{com}}$ for RS-ModCubes are computed as:

$$ {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathbf{M}_{rsm}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{m}_{i},\quad\mathbf{r_{com}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{m}_{i}\mathbf{p}_{i}}{\mathbf{M}_{rsm}},\quad\mathbf{r}_{i}=\mathbf{p}_{i}-\mathbf{r_{com}}} $$

where $\mathbf{p}_{i}$ and $\mathbf{m}_{i}$ are position vector and mass of the $i$ -th ModCube module, respectively. $N$ is the number of ModCube module. $\mathbf{r}_{i}$ is the relative position of each ModCube module with respect to CoM of RS-ModCubes. Applying the parallel axis theorem, the updated total inertia tensor $\mathbf{I}_{rsm}$ of RS-ModCubes is:

$$ \mathbf{I}_{rsm}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\mathbf{I}_{i}+\mathbf{m}_{i}\left(\|\mathbf{r}_{i}\|^{2}\mathbf{I}_{3}-\mathbf{r}_{i}\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\top}\right)\right) $$

where, $\mathbf{I}_{i}$ is the inertia tensor of the $i$ -th ModCube module about its own CoM, and $\mathbf{I}_{3}$ is the $3\times 3$ identity matrix.

The total mass matrix $\mathbf{M}_{rsm}$ and the coriolis and centripetal matrix $\mathbf{C}_{rsm}(\boldsymbol{\nu})$ for RS-ModCubes are then given by:

$$ {\mathbf{M}_{rsm}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{M}_{rsm}\mathbf{I}_{3}&-\mathbf{M}_{rsm}{\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\times}}^{\top}\\
\mathbf{M}_{rsm}{\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\times}}&\mathbf{I}_{rsm}\end{bmatrix}+\mathbf{M}_{A}} $$

$$ \mathbf{C}_{rsm}(\mathbf{v},\omega)=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{0}_{3\times 3}&-\mathbf{M}_{rsm}\boldsymbol{\mathbf{v}}^{\times}-{\mathbf{M}_{A}\mathbf{v}}^{\times}\\
\mathbf{M}_{rsm}\boldsymbol{\mathbf{v}}^{\times}+{\mathbf{M}_{A}\mathbf{v}}^{\times}&{(\mathbf{I}_{rsm}\omega)}^{\times}+{(\mathbf{M}_{A}\omega)}^{\times}\end{bmatrix} $$

where, parameters marked with $\{^{\times}\}$ represent the skew-symmetric matrix form of the corresponding vector. $\mathbf{M}_{A}$ denotes the added mass matrix, which is designed to be zero.

Finally, the dynamics of RS-ModCubes are described by:

$$ \mathbf{M}_{rsm}\dot{\boldsymbol{\nu}}+\mathbf{C}_{rsm}(\boldsymbol{\nu})\boldsymbol{\nu}+\boldsymbol{D}_{rsm,lut}(\boldsymbol{\nu})\boldsymbol{\nu}=\boldsymbol{\tau} $$

The control law for RS-ModCubes is same to Eq. 3, giving as:

$$ \displaystyle\boldsymbol{\tau} \displaystyle=K_{P}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}+K_{D}\dot{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\eta}}}+\mathbf{M}_{rsm}\dot{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{m}+\mathbf{C}_{rsm}({\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{m})\boldsymbol{\nu}_{m} \displaystyle\quad+\boldsymbol{D}_{rsm,lut}(\boldsymbol{\nu}_{m})\boldsymbol{\nu}_{m} $$

## VI Evaluation of Actuation Capability and Power Efficiency

### VI-A Reachable Wrench Space

To evaluate the robot’s capability to generate wrenches in various directions, we formulate a convex optimization problem to determine the reachable wrench space. $\Omega_{W}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n_{s}}\{(\mathbf{\tau}_{n}=\lambda P_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{6}\mid\mathbf{\lambda}\geq 0,\{\mathcal{B}\}\}$ , $P_{d}$ and $n_{s}$ defined in Algorithm 1 (line 3–5). $\mathbf{\tau}_{n}$ is the net wrench. The optimization problem defined as:

$$ \displaystyle\max \displaystyle\lambda_{j},\quad j\in n_{s} \displaystyle\text{subject to} \displaystyle{\displaystyle J_{t}}\,{F_{T}}=\lambda_{j}P_{d},\quad Eq.\ref{eq:Jacobian}, \displaystyle F_{t,\min}\leq F_{t,i}\leq F_{t,\max}\mid F_{t,i}\in F_{T},i\in n_{t} $$

where, the thrust matrix ${F_{T}}$ and thruster number $n_{t}$ from Eq. 5. The reachable wrench spaces of seven different vehicles are shown in Fig. 5 (second to last line). Additionally, the volume of the Maximum Inscribed Ellipsoid (MIE), denoted as $V_{MIE}$ , illustrates the maximum stable wrench task space [23]. The corresponding $V_{MIE}$ values are provided in Table I, and visualized inside wrench space.

### VI-B Morphological Characterization

To evaluate the parameter spaces $\Omega_{W}$ and $\Omega_{P}$ , we analyze the relative Willmore energy ( $E_{\mathcal{W}}$ ) and Dirichlet energy ( $E_{D}$ ), which offer insights into smoothness, continuity, and transition stability. Additionally, the variance in thrusters’ effort serves as a key metric for assessing individual lifespan.

$E_{\mathcal{W}}$ is calculated by:

$$ E_{\mathcal{W}}({\Omega})=\int_{{\Omega}}H^{2}\,dA-\int_{{\Omega}}K\,da $$

$H$ denotes the mean curvature at a vertex sample point $\{{p}_{i}\in P_{d}\mid i\in n_{s}\}$ , where the set of points is derived from Algorithm 1. Here, $K$ represents the Gaussian curvature at $p_{i}$ , and $a$ is the differential surface area element associated with $p_{i}$ .

$E_{\mathcal{D}}$ is calculated as:

$$ E_{\mathcal{D}}=\sum_{l=0}^{l_{\text{max}}}\sum_{m=-l}^{l}l(l+1)\left|\arg\min_{a}\|Ya-r\|_{2}\right|^{2} $$

where $r$ is the radial distance of the vertices from the centroid in spherical coordinates, and $Y$ is the matrix of spherical harmonic basis functions $Y_{l}^{m}(\theta,\phi)$ representing the surface geometry. The coefficients $a$ are obtained by solving the least-squares problem $\arg\min_{a}\|Ya-r\|_{2}$ . $l_{\text{max}}=10$ is the maximum harmonic degree, and $l(l+1)$ is a weighting factor that penalizes higher-order harmonics to prioritize surface smoothness.

### VII-D Trajectory Planning for RS-ModCubes

RS-ModCubes trajectories are planned using the Minimum Snap method [24], which minimizes the total snap (fourth derivative of position) over a piecewise polynomial path to ensure smooth trajectory generation. Each segment $k$ of the trajectory is represented as a polynomial: $p_{k}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\alpha_{k,i}\,(t-t_{k-1})^{i},$ where $t_{k-1}$ is the start time of segment $k$ , $\alpha_{k,i}$ are coefficients, and $n$ is the polynomial order. The optimization problem defined as:

$$ \displaystyle\min \displaystyle J=\sum_{k=1}^{M}\int_{0}^{T_{k}}\left(\frac{d^{4}p_{k}(t)}{dt^{4}}\right)^{2}dt \displaystyle\text{subject to} \displaystyle p_{k}(0)=w_{j},\quad p_{k}(T_{k})=w_{j+1}, \displaystyle\frac{d^{m}p_{k}(T_{k})}{dt^{m}}=\frac{d^{m}p_{k+1}(0)}{dt^{m}},\quad m\in\{0,1,2\} $$

where $w_{j}$ and $w_{j+1}$ are waypoints, and $T_{k}$ is the duration of segment $k$ . The constraints enforce boundary conditions at waypoints and continuity up to the second derivative (acceleration) between segments. We utilize the OSQP solver to address the optimization problem. ## VIII Conclusion and Future Works

This work introduces a reconfigurable and scalable underwater robot system, RS-ModCubes. Experimental results demonstrate precise trajectory tracking and stable docking, highlighting robustness in both individual and multi-module configurations, even in constrained environments. Morphological characterization results, reveal the system’s advantages in actuation distribution and energy efficiency compared to four commercial underwater robots, with reconfiguration enabling modulation of dynamic capabilities.

Future work will focus on: (1) Expanding swarm scalability beyond four modules to enable advanced coordination and complex formations, (2) Enhancing control and planning by integrating collision avoidance and more robust vision-based localization for improved precision and adaptability, and (3) Developing decentralized, task-specific reconfiguration policies to facilitate large-scale swarm operations and applications.

**Authors:** Er-Chuang Li; Tian-Yi Zhang; Meng-Ting Cai; Sheng-Yao Su; Chun-Hong Shen; Qi-Lun Lai; Yin-Xi Zhang

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Neurology, Taikang Ningbo Hospital; | 2Department of Neurology, First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Zhejiang University; | 3Department of Neurology, Second Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Zhejiang University; and | 4Department of Neurology, Zhejiang Hospital, China.

## Abstract

In dipeptidyl-peptidase-like protein 6 (DPPX) antibody-associated encephalitis, DPPX antibodies from serum and CSF target the extracellular subunit of the voltage-gated potassium channel 4.2. This targeting leads to a characteristic clinical triad comprising gastrointestinal symptoms (predominantly diarrhea), cognitive-psychiatric dysfunction, and manifestations of CNS hyperexcitability, with hyperekplexia being a more specific feature. This rare disease typically presents with a subacute or chronic course and often affects middle-aged and older individuals. Patients may have a weak association with certain hematologic malignancies, particularly lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Brain MRI typically shows normal findings or nonspecific white matter changes. DPPX antibody-associated encephalitis responds well to immunotherapy, and most patients ultimately present with a good prognosis. However, relapses can occur. To improve our understanding of this rare but treatable autoimmune encephalitis and avoid misdiagnosis, we conduct a systematic review and summarize the current knowledge of its clinical and paraclinical features, management, and prognosis.

## Introduction

Following the description of 4 patients characterized by frequent prodromal diarrhea, prominent manifestations of CNS hyperexcitability (hyperekplexia, seizures, myoclonus, tremors), the presence of dipeptidyl-peptidase-like protein 6 (DPPX or DPP6) antibody in CSF/serum, and improvement after immunotherapy in 2013, Boronat et al. named this novel inflammatory disease “DPPX antibody-associated encephalitis (DPPXE).”1,2 This rare but treatable disease typically has an insidious onset, often progresses chronically or subacutely, and affects multiple systems with notable symptom heterogeneity.2 The publication of additional case reports and small case series has facilitated the discovery of uncommon manifestations, thereby broadening the recognized clinical spectrum of DPPXE. In this systematic review, we aim to expand on the 10-year findings and summarize recent advances to enhance contemporary understanding.

## Methods

### Search Strategy

In accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines,3 3 investigators (E.C.L., T.Y.Z., M.T.C.) conducted independent searches for literature from January 2013 to May 2024 in PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane. The following search terms were used: (dipeptidyl-peptidase-like protein 6 OR DPPX OR DPP6 OR dipeptidyl-peptidase-like protein 6 antibody OR DPPX antibody OR DPP6 antibody OR anti-dipeptidyl-peptidase-like protein 6 antibody OR anti-DPPX antibody OR anti-DPP6 antibody) AND (encephalitis OR autoimmune encephalitis OR AE). A manual search was also performed for additional relevant studies using references cited in the included articles. Disagreements in screening were settled through discussion.

### Study Selection and Data Extraction

We included all English publications reporting DPPXE, encompassing case reports and case series. The exclusion criteria were defined as follows: (1) conference abstracts or review articles; (2) full articles with restricted access; (3) nonhuman studies; (4) case reports or case series without detailed clinical data; (5) repetitive cases described in a previous publication. Data extraction was separately performed by 3 researchers (E.C.L., T.Y.Z., M.T.C.). Demographic, clinical, paraclinical, treatment, and outcome data were collected. Potential discrepancies were resolved by consensus with other authors.

### Statistical Analysis

For descriptive statistics, categorical variables were expressed as percentages and quantitative variables as medians (ranges or interquartile ranges [IQRs]). Intergroup comparisons of categorical variables were analyzed using a χ2 test or Fisher exact test. The p value of <0.05 was considered as statistically significant. All the analyses were performed with SPSS version 21.0.

## Results and Discussion

The PRISMA flowchart is displayed in Figure 1. A total of 104 patients with DPPXE were identified from 11 case series (82 patients)1,2,4-12 and 22 individual case reports (22 patients).13-34 Notably, more than 2/5 of these cases were reported in China (42/104, 40.4%), followed by the United States (38/104, 36.5%), Spain (12/104, 11.5%), and Germany (7/104, 6.7%).

### Etiology

The actual cause of DPPXE remains poorly understood, and most patients lacked specific disease-initiating triggers. A few patients developed DPPXE after potential viral infections (e.g., herpes simplex virus-1 infection) or Leptospira infection.11,21,32 Immune checkpoint inhibitor (sintilimab) was reported as a potential trigger in one patient.34

In addition, 13.5% (14/104) of patients with DPPXE had associated malignant tumors (eTable 1), with hematologic cancers being the most common (lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia), followed by solid malignancies such as breast adenocarcinoma, liver cancer, gastric cancer, and micropapillary carcinoma of thyroid.2,4,8-11,16,18,23,31,34 Neoplasms could occur before or after (up to 2.5 years) the diagnosis of DPPXE.8,16,18,23,31 Notably, some patients experienced symptomatic improvement after cancer treatment, suggesting that tumors might be an underlying trigger for this disease.4,18 We compared the clinical and paraclinical findings in patients with tumors vs those without tumors and found that the presence of MRI abnormality was associated with concomitant tumors (9/10 vs 31/85, p = 0.004) (eTable 2). Although DPPX antibody is classified as a lower risk antibody for paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome,35 comprehensive cancer screening during the initial assessment is still recommended, especially in patients with MRI abnormalities.

### Clinical Presentations

DPPXE mainly affected middle-aged and older individuals (median onset age: 52.5 years; range: 11–80 years) with a male predominance (M:F ratio of 1.9:1). There were no significant differences in clinical features between the male and female groups (eTable 3). The main clinical manifestations of DPPXE are summarized in eTable 1. Approximately 44.2% (41/104) of patients presented with a triad of gastrointestinal symptoms (predominately diarrhea), cognitive-psychiatric dysfunction, and manifestation of CNS hyperexcitability. Notably, DPPXE could coexist with other autoimmune diseases such as hypothyroidism, systemic lupus erythematosus, and type 1 diabetes mellitus (Figure 2).4,9,11

#### CNS Manifestations

Cognitive deficits occurred in 70.2% (73/104) of patients with DPPXE. Memory decline (58.7%, 61/104) was the most common symptom, followed by disorientation, executive dysfunction, impaired attention, agnosia, aphasia, and apraxia. Around 40.4% (42/104) of the patients experienced psychiatric symptoms, mainly visual and auditory hallucinations, loss of concentration, depression, delusions, irritability, or reticence.

CNS hyperexcitability, a prominent pathophysiologic phenomenon, occurred in 63.5% (66/104) of patients with DPPXE. Core manifestations included myoclonus (possibly cortical origin; could occur at night), tremors (action or static), hyperekplexia, seizure, and rigidity/stiffness. Among these, hyperekplexia was a more specific feature, typically presenting as a diffuse, nonhabituating, and exaggerated startle response of the trunk and limbs to accidental or repetitive acoustic or tactile stimuli. It could be accompanied by synchronous, symmetrical myoclonus of the limbs and spasms of the head, neck, and trunk, triggered even by mild stimuli such as a breeze, visual stimulation, the examiner's breath, or routine procedures.2,5

Approximately 40.4% (42/104) of patients with DPPXE experienced brainstem or cerebellar dysfunction, with cerebellar ataxia (36.5%, 38/104) and nystagmus (25.0%, 26/104) being the most common. However, a minority of patients might also develop severe respiratory failure as a complication, which should be given clinical attention.

Sleep disturbances, such as insomnia and hypersomnia, were observed in approximately 41.3% (43/104) of patients with DPPXE. In a study, 6 patients from Mayo Clinic underwent evaluation using video-polysomnography, which revealed REM sleep-atonia loss and ambiguous sleep with status dissociatus.10 They identified the prominent sleep problems to be sleep-disordered breathing, REM sleep behavior disorder, and abnormalities in non-REM sleep architecture. Although sleep symptoms are rarely the primary presenting concern in patients with DPPXE, often overshadowed by other neurologic and psychiatric issues, they can be readily identified when inquired about directly.

#### Autonomic Symptoms

Gastrointestinal abnormalities (with diarrhea and abdominal pain being the most common) were reported in 54.8% (57/104) of patients with DPPXE, typically manifesting as initial symptoms. In 16 patients with available information, diarrhea began a median of 5.5 months (range: 1–180 months) preceding the onset of neurologic symptoms. Furthermore, 50.0% (52/104) of patients experienced prominent weight loss (predominantly related to diarrhea). The median weight reduction was 25 kg (range: 5–180 kg) in 36 patients with accessible data. Constipation, gastroparesis, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting were also observed during the disease course. In addition, other nongastrointestinal autonomic symptoms occurred in 18.3% (19/104) of patients, for instance, urinary problems, erectile dysfunction, and orthostatic hypotension.

### Paraclinical Investigations

#### MRI

Only 42.1% (40/95) of patients with available brain MRI scans showed abnormalities (eTable 4). Nonspecific white matter changes were the most common finding, followed by T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensities with or without contrast enhancement in the cerebellum, temporal lobe, brainstem, and basal ganglia (Figure 3). By analyzing the accessible clinical characteristics in patients with MRI abnormalities vs those without abnormalities, we found that the presence of tumors (8/31 vs 1/39, p = 0.012) and EEG abnormalities (10/13 vs 8/22, p = 0.035) were associated with abnormal MRI findings (eTable 5). However, no significant differences in clinical features, outcomes, or coexisting tumors were observed between patients with abnormal and normal MRI findings. Of interest, a previous pooled analysis suggested that MRI abnormalities specific for encephalitis might be more common in Chinese patients compared with non-Chinese patients.8

#### Positron Emission Tomography (PET)

In total, 50.0% (11/22) of patients with available PET (including 18-fluorodeoxyglucose [18F-FDG] and translocator protein [TSPO]) scans had detectable abnormalities, including 18F-FDG hypometabolism and hypermetabolism, and increased TSPO uptake in focal regions of the brain. PET seemed to be more sensitive than conventional MRI sequences in detecting intracranial lesions in patients with DPPXE,12,21 although there was a mismatch between brain regions showing abnormalities on MRI and those exhibiting abnormal PET metabolism. However, the limited sample size restricts the assessment of the diagnostic specificity of PET scans for this specific condition.

#### Serum and CSF Analysis

Routine laboratory blood tests were typically unremarkable. However, CSF analysis often revealed inflammatory findings (eTable 4). In the patients who underwent lumbar puncture, more than half showed CSF abnormalities, covering pleocytosis (median: 15 cells/μL, range: 6–370 cells/μL, primarily lymphocytes, data available for 21 cases), increased protein levels (median: 74 mg/dL, range: 46.0–209.6 mg/dL, data available for 23 cases), positive oligoclonal bands, and elevated immunoglobulin G (IgG) index (>0.7).

#### Antibody Detection

A combination of cell-based assay (CBA) and tissue-based assay (TBA) is generally recommended for accurate antibody detection; nevertheless, positivity by commercially available CBA in both serum and CSF would suffice to make a diagnosis (without TBA). IgG1 and IgG4 were the most frequently identified subclasses of DPPX antibodies (IgG1–4).2 A study in the United States reported a median DPPX antibody level by CBA in serum to be 1:15,360 (range: 1920–245760), significantly higher than that in CSF (1:64; range: 2–128).4 However, a case series from China found a median DPPX antibody level by CBA in serum and CSF to be 1:32 (range: 10–1,000) and 1:3.2 (range: 1–10), respectively.8 These discrepancies between studies may be primarily due to differences in ethnicity or the timing of detection during the disease course. The relationship between antibody levels and disease severity or relapse is yet to be determined. A previous study suggested suggested that serum DPPX antibody levels seemed to be as useful for diagnosing DPPXE as CSF levels,4 but considering that DPPX antibodies were often synthesized intrathecally, CSF antibody testing could be more specific than serum testing. The diagnostic value of a positive serum test alone remains uncertain. If paired testing is unavailable, CSF testing is preferred because of its higher specificity. It should be noted that when a patient's neurologic presentation does not align with the presence of DPPX antibodies, particularly at low titers (with no defined cutoff yet established), a critical evaluation of the antibody results is warranted.

Nine patients with DPPXE also had antibodies to other neural antigens,4,7,8,11,12,18,33 as presented in Figure 2. When interpreting these findings, it is crucial to consider the specific clinical presentation (phenotype) associated with each antibody to avoid misdiagnosis due to the presence of multiple antibodies. Four additional patients with DPPXE had systemic autoantibodies,1,4,7,23 which suggests the possibility of coexisting autoimmune diseases.

### Neuropathology

There is a scarcity of pathologic studies on DPPXE. Biopsies of gastrointestinal tissue revealed nonspecific inflammatory changes.14 An autopsy demonstrated patchy neuronal loss in the cerebellum, hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, and temporo-occipital cortex. In addition, there was activation of microglia. Routine immunohistochemical staining showed inflammatory infiltration of scattered CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, with isolated CD20+ B cells. Notably, there were no deposits of complement or plasma cells.36

### Management

Owing to the rarity of DPPXE, there are currently no evidence-based guidelines or established consensus for treatment. Immunosuppression remains the mainstay of therapy, and oncotherapy is also crucial for some patients with concomitant tumors.

#### Immunotherapy

Among the 104 patients with DPPXE, 90.4% (94/104) received immunotherapeutic agents and 77.9% (81/104) had detailed treatment regimens. In all cases with detailed treatment regimens (100.0%, 81/81), first-line immunotherapies were administered early in the disease course. IV methylprednisolone (IVMP) was preferred (77/81; 1,000 mg for a 3–5 days with a tapering schedule), followed by IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) (37/81; 0.4 g/kg per day for 5 days) and plasma exchange (PLEX) (33/81; 5–7 sessions over 7–14 days). Combination immunotherapies with IVIG plus IVMP or IVMP plus PLEX were frequently used. The optimal duration of corticosteroid treatment is yet to be determined, but a 3–6 month course may be reasonable.

Approximately 59.3% (48/81) of patients received second-line immunotherapies, including rituximab (RTX) (36/81), cyclophosphamide (11/81), mycophenolate mofetil (10/81), and azathioprine (7/81). Patients who received RTX tended to have a good outcome (modified Rankin Scale [mRS] score, 0–2) compared with those who did not (22/45 vs 4/13, p = 0.247). Based on this finding, for patients with DPPXE, particularly those with coexisting B-cell neoplasm, the combination of RTX with steroids and IVIG/PLEX could be a better treatment option.

There is still debate about the necessity and duration of maintenance therapy. Considering it a potentially chronic disease, long-term therapy may be beneficial, especially for patients with risk factors of relapse. Currently, the general recommendation for the maintenance treatment of autoimmune encephalitis suggests initial long-term immunosuppression, with a preference for RTX, for a duration of 3 years, followed by reevaluation and an attempt to withdraw immunotherapy.37 Therefore, it could be reasonable to apply this in DPPXE. However, the existing data are insufficient to provide definitive recommendations.

#### Oncotherapy

Treatment of underlying tumors seems to be equally effective as immunotherapy in preventing the progression of neurologic deficits and improving the prognosis.16,18 Among the 14 patients with concomitant tumors, 71.4% (10/14) received oncotherapy, including chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and/or tumor resection.

### Clinical Outcomes

Most patients with DPPXE responded favorably to immunotherapy and/or oncotherapy. Among patients who received immunotherapy and/or oncotherapy, 9.6% (9/94) experienced progressive neurologic decline (including death), 7.4% (7/94) stabilized, and 82.9% (78/94) exhibited improvement. Finally, follow-up mRS scores were documented in 72 of the 104 patients. The median follow-up time was 12 months (range: 1–196 months), and the median mRS score was 2 (range: 0–6, IQR: 1–2), indicating a generally good prognosis. In an effort to identify factors associated with poorer prognosis, we compared the clinical and paraclinical features of patients who fell into these 2 outcome categories (Table 1). A clinical triad was more frequent in the poor prognosis group (12/16 patients) compared with the good prognosis group (18/56 patients) (p = 0.002).

Approximately 28.7% (27/94) of patients experienced relapses. Nevertheless, the relapse rate was likely an underestimate because some patients were lost to follow-up or the clinical visit time was insufficient. We observed that patients with relapses had a longer follow-up period (median: 24 months; range: 4–196 months) compared with those without relapses (median: 6 months; range: 1–112 months). This discrepancy could result in an underestimation of the relapse rate because patients who had not yet relapsed might do so during a more extended follow-up. Furthermore, the implementation of maintenance therapy was another factor that can influence relapse rates. From the available data analysis, relapses were more frequent in patients presenting with cerebellar ataxia, CSF abnormalities, and positive antibodies in serum and CSF or lacking first-line treatment, indicating these parameters as potential risk factors of reoccurrence (Table 2).

Some patients were reported to experience long-term sequelae, such as gait instability and cognitive deficits. The overall mortality rate for patients with DPPXE was 5.8% (6/104) with a mean follow-up of 12 months (range: 1–196 months). These deaths were primarily due to medical complications, such as pneumonia associated with bulbar dysfunction.5,36

## Conclusions

In the past decade, significant progress has been made in understanding DPPXE. A triad of gastrointestinal symptoms (predominantly diarrhea), cognitive dysfunction, and manifestations of CNS hyperexcitability should raise suspicion for DPPXE. The strongest diagnostic evidence comes from the detection of DPPX antibodies in both serum and CSF. Fortunately, most patients respond well to immunotherapy and have a favorable long-term prognosis, although relapses can occur. We expect that a larger number of well-characterized DPPXE cases will not only broaden the recognized clinical spectrum of the disease but also pave the way for standardized diagnostic and treatment guidelines in the future.
